title: Volume and pitch: what makes a sound loud or quiet, high or low

summary.text: Pluck a string gently, then hard. The sound gets louder, but the note stays the same. Now hang a heavier weight on the string. The note rises, and the loudness hardly changes. So every sound has two separate measures. Volume is how loud it is, and it comes from the size of the vibration. Pitch is how high or low it is, and it comes from the number of vibrations each second. In this unit you measure both. You find three ways to change the pitch of a string. You find several ways to make a sound louder or quieter. You also find out which of the two measures reaches a far listener unchanged.
summary.art: One string drawn twice between two pencils: on the left as a narrow blur and a wide blur with the same musical note above both, on the right hung with a small bottle and a large bottle with a low note and a high note above them.

intro.hook: A mosquito near your ear is quiet, and her whine is high. A chenda drum across a temple yard is loud, and its beat is low. If you hit the chenda harder, will its note go higher? If the mosquito comes closer, will her whine go lower?
intro.text: Both answers are no. Hitting harder makes the drum louder, and its note stays where it was. Coming closer makes the whine louder, and it stays just as high. Loud and high are two different things, and different changes move them. In this unit you build one string on a table and test it with a bottle of water. You measure its loudness in decibels and its note in hertz. Then you wrap a ringing phone in a towel and find what the towel changes and what it leaves alone.
intro.art: A small mosquito beside a child's ear on the left and a large chenda drum far across a temple yard on the right, with a small high note above the mosquito and a large low note above the drum.

outcomes: I can describe any sound with two measures, its volume and its pitch, and tell them apart.
I can link volume to amplitude and pitch to frequency, and name their units, the decibel and the hertz.
I can read the decibel scale, and say why sounds above 85 decibels can harm hearing.
I can make the pitch of a string higher or lower in three ways, and explain each one.
I can explain how air columns and skins change pitch, and how the three families of instruments are played.
I can make a sound louder or quieter, and say where the energy comes from or goes.
I can plan a fair test, name its variables, and repeat my measurements.
I can explain why pitch reaches a far listener unchanged, and volume does not.

terms.meaning: How loud or quiet a sound is. Volume depends on how much energy the sound brings to your ear each second.
terms.example: A whisper has a low volume. A pressure cooker whistle has a high volume.
terms.art: A row of five sound sources from a falling leaf to a pressure cooker, with a bar under each that grows taller from left to right.

terms.meaning: How high or low a note sounds. Pitch depends on how many vibrations reach your ear each second.
terms.example: A mosquito's whine has a high pitch. A chenda's beat has a low pitch.
terms.art: A ladder with a small bird singing at the top rung and a large drum at the bottom rung.

terms.meaning: How far a vibrating thing moves from its rest position. A bigger amplitude gives a louder sound.
terms.example: In Gentle Pluck, Hard Pluck, you pull a string aside by half a centimetre, then by 2 centimetres. The second pull has four times the amplitude.
terms.art: A string between two pencils drawn as a narrow blur and as a wide blur, each with an arrow from the middle line to the edge of the blur.

terms.meaning: The number of vibrations in one second. A higher frequency gives a higher pitch.
terms.example: A string that moves back and forth 220 times each second has a frequency of 220 hertz.
terms.art: A stopwatch showing one second beside a string, with small tally marks counting its trips.

terms.meaning: The unit of frequency. One hertz is one vibration each second. It is written Hz for short.
terms.example: A tuner app shows the frequency of a plucked string in hertz.
terms.art: A phone screen showing the number 220 and the letters Hz, held near a string.

terms.meaning: The unit of volume. It is written dB for short. Every 10 decibels more means ten times as much sound energy.
terms.example: Talking at one metre is about 60 decibels. A mixie one metre away is about 85 to 90 decibels.
terms.art: A tall scale marked from 0 to 120 with small pictures beside it: a leaf at 20, two people talking at 60, a mixie at 90.

terms.meaning: A tool that measures volume in decibels. A free app turns a phone into a rough one.
terms.example: In the Muffle Test, a phone with a sound meter app sits 50 centimetres from a ringing phone.
terms.art: A phone lying on a book with a dial on its screen pointing at 66 dB.

terms.meaning: How hard a string or a skin is pulled tight. More tension gives a higher pitch.
terms.example: In the Water-Bottle String, a bottle of water hangs from the string. More water gives more tension.
terms.art: A string running over a table edge with a water bottle hanging from it, and an arrow along the string labelled 'tension'.

terms.meaning: The air inside a tube or a bottle. It vibrates when you blow across it or into it. A shorter air column gives a higher pitch.
terms.example: In the Filling Bottle, the air column above the water gets shorter as the bottle fills.
terms.art: A bottle half full of water, with the air above the water shaded and a ruler beside it.

terms.meaning: A wide, thin surface that vibrates with a string and pushes a lot of air. It makes the sound louder without adding energy.
terms.example: The hollow wooden body of a veena is its soundboard. A wooden table does the same for the Water-Bottle String.
terms.art: A thin string pushing a few dots of air, and beside it the wide face of a veena pushing many dots of air.

terms.meaning: To make a sound quieter by covering its source, or by putting something in its path.
terms.example: A phone ringing under a pillow is muffled.
terms.art: A phone under a pillow with small faint sound lines coming out.

terms.meaning: To take in. A soft, thick material absorbs sound: the vibration gets into it and ends up as a tiny amount of warmth.
terms.example: Thick curtains and cushioned seats absorb sound in a cinema hall.
terms.art: Sound lines entering a thick folded towel and fading away inside it.

terms.meaning: An electric machine that makes a weak signal from a microphone stronger. It adds energy from a battery or the mains.
terms.example: At a kutcheri, the singer's microphone is joined to an amplifier.
terms.art: A microphone joined by a wire to a box with a knob, joined by another wire to a loudspeaker.

terms.meaning: A machine that turns an electric signal into sound. The signal pushes a stiff cone back and forth, and the cone pushes the air.
terms.example: A phone has a loudspeaker smaller than your fingernail. A festival stage has ones as tall as a door.
terms.art: A cut-away loudspeaker showing its cone, with arrows showing the cone moving in and out.

terms.meaning: An instrument in which tight strings vibrate. The player changes the pitch by changing the length or the tension of a string.
terms.example: The veena, the sitar, the violin and the ektara are string instruments.
terms.art: A veena, a violin and an ektara side by side.

terms.meaning: An instrument in which an air column vibrates. The player changes the pitch by making the air column longer or shorter.
terms.example: The bansuri, the nadaswaram and the shehnai are wind instruments.
terms.art: A bansuri, a nadaswaram and a conch side by side.

terms.meaning: An instrument that is struck, shaken or scraped. In a drum, a tight skin vibrates.
terms.example: The mridangam, the tabla, the kanjira and the ghatam are percussion instruments.
terms.art: A mridangam, a kanjira and a clay ghatam side by side.

terms.meaning: Sound that someone does not want, or sound loud enough to harm. The same sound can be music to one listener and noise to another.
terms.example: A loudspeaker at midnight is noise to a sleeping baby and to the birds roosting nearby.
terms.art: A loudspeaker on a pole at night beside a window where a baby sleeps and a tree where birds roost.

terms.meaning: Infrasound has a frequency below 20 hertz, too low for humans to hear. Ultrasound is above 20,000 hertz, too high for humans to hear.
terms.example: Elephants call to each other with infrasound. Bats find insects with ultrasound.
terms.art: A scale of frequency with an elephant below the 20 mark, a child in the middle part and a bat above the 20,000 mark.

terms.meaning: The one thing you change on purpose in a fair test.
terms.example: In the Water-Bottle String, the independent variable is the amount of water in the bottle.
terms.art: Three bottles holding different amounts of water, with a hand pointing at them.

terms.meaning: The thing you measure in a fair test. It depends on what you changed.
terms.example: In the Water-Bottle String, the dependent variable is the frequency of the note.
terms.art: A phone screen showing a number in hertz, with an eye looking at it.

terms.meaning: The things you keep the same in a fair test, so that only one thing changes.
terms.example: In the Water-Bottle String, the string, its length and the place you pluck stay the same.
terms.art: A string, a ruler and two pencils, each marked with a small padlock.

explanations.concept: Every sound has a volume and a pitch
explanations.definition: Volume is how loud or quiet a sound is. Pitch is how high or low it is. The two are separate, and each can change while the other stays the same.
explanations.description: Think of two questions you can ask about any sound. How loud is it? How high is it? A mosquito's whine is quiet and high. A chenda's beat is loud and low. A pressure cooker whistle is loud and high, and a cat's purr is quiet and low. So all four mixes exist. In Four Hums, you hum a low note softly and then strongly. You do the same with a high note. Your throat can change the loudness and leave the note alone. It can also change the note and leave the loudness alone. This tells you that two different things are being changed. The next cards say what they are.
examples: A lullaby and a shout can be sung on the same note. Only the volume differs.
Sa and the higher Pa can be sung equally softly. Only the pitch differs.
On a harmonium, each key gives one pitch. Pumping the bellows harder changes only the volume.
explanations.art: A square divided into four boxes with a mosquito, a pressure cooker, a purring cat and a chenda drum, one in each box, with 'quiet to loud' along the bottom and 'low to high' up the side.

explanations.concept: Volume comes from the amplitude of the vibration
explanations.definition: A bigger vibration pushes the air harder and gives the sound more energy. More energy reaching your ear each second means a louder sound.
explanations.description: The amplitude of a vibration is how far the thing moves from its rest position. In Gentle Pluck, Hard Pluck, you pull a string aside by half a centimetre, 1 centimetre and 2 centimetres. The bigger pull gives a wider blur and a louder sound. The reason is energy. Your finger does more work to pull the string further, so the string starts with more energy. A string that swings wider pushes the air harder, and the air carries more energy to your ear. The frequency does not change. The string makes bigger trips in the same time, so it must move faster on each trip. As the sound dies away, the blur gets narrower and the note stays the same.
examples: Hitting a mridangam harder makes the skin move further, and the beat is louder.
Blowing more air through a whistle makes the air inside it vibrate more strongly.
Each time the amplitude doubles, the meter reads about 6 decibels more.
explanations.art: The same string drawn three times with a narrow, a medium and a wide blur, and a sound meter beside each showing a higher number for the wider blur.

explanations.definition: Volume is measured in decibels. Every 10 decibels more means ten times as much sound energy, and it sounds about twice as loud.
explanations.description: The quietest sound a young person can hear is called 0 decibels. Leaves rustling are about 20 decibels, and a whisper is about 30. Talking at one metre is about 60. A mixie at one metre is about 85 to 90, and a motorcycle horn close by is about 100. The scale grows by multiplying. A sound of 70 decibels has ten times the energy of a sound of 60. A sound of 80 has a hundred times the energy. Yet 70 decibels sounds only about twice as loud as 60 to most people. This is why two singers are not twice as loud as one. Two equal sounds together read only 3 decibels more than one. Sounds above 85 decibels can harm the hair cells in the inner ear if you hear them for hours. The louder the sound, the shorter the safe time. In India, the Noise Pollution Rules of 2000 set a daytime limit of 55 decibels for places where people live.
examples: A sound meter app in a quiet bedroom at night reads about 30 to 40 decibels.
Ten people talking at once read about 70 decibels, which is 10 more than one person.
Earplugs or earmuffs lower the sound that reaches the ear by about 15 to 30 decibels.
explanations.art: A vertical decibel scale from 0 to 120 with a leaf, a whisper, two people talking, a mixie and a motorcycle horn at their places, and a red band above 85.

explanations.concept: Pitch comes from the frequency of the vibration
explanations.definition: Frequency is the number of vibrations each second, measured in hertz. A higher frequency gives a higher pitch.
explanations.description: Each vibration gives the air one push. A string that vibrates 220 times a second sends 220 pushes a second to your ear. Your ear and brain do not count them. You hear how often they come as a pitch. A tuner app can count them, and it shows the frequency in hertz. A young person can hear from about 20 hertz up to about 20,000 hertz. A man's speaking voice is about 120 hertz, and a woman's is about 210. Other animals hear different ranges. An elephant hears and makes sounds below 20 hertz, called infrasound. A dog hears up to about 45,000 hertz, and many bats hear above 100,000. Sound above 20,000 hertz is called ultrasound.
examples: The note A that orchestras tune to is 440 hertz.
A mosquito's wings beat about 500 times a second, so her whine is about 500 hertz.
A field cricket's chirp is about 5,000 hertz, which is why it sounds so thin and high.
explanations.art: A line of frequency from 20 to 20,000 hertz with an elephant at the low end, a man and a woman talking in the low middle, a cricket in the high middle and a bat past the high end.

explanations.concept: Three ways to change the pitch of a string
explanations.definition: A string gives a higher pitch when it is tighter, shorter or lighter. It gives a lower pitch when it is looser, longer or heavier.
explanations.description: A tighter string is pulled back to its rest position harder, so each trip takes less time. In the Water-Bottle String, more water in the hanging bottle gives a higher note. But twice the pull does not give twice the frequency. It takes four times the pull to double the frequency, and nine times to make it three times as high. A shorter string has less distance to cover and less of itself to move. Half the length gives twice the frequency. A heavier string has more to move, so each trip takes longer. A string with a second strand wound round it gives a lower note than the string alone. The French scientist Marin Mersenne published these three rules in 1636. A veena player uses all three. The thick strings are for low notes. The pegs change the tension. Pressing a string on a fret makes the vibrating part shorter.
examples: A guitar's six strings are the same length. The thick ones are tuned low and the thin ones high.
A veena player pulls a string sideways across a fret. This tightens the string and slides the note up.
When you sing higher, small muscles stretch the vocal folds in your throat tighter and thinner.
explanations.art: One string shown three ways: with a small and a large hanging bottle, with two pencils far apart and close together, and as one strand and a strand with a second wound round it, each pair marked 'lower' and 'higher'.

explanations.concept: How air columns and skins change pitch
explanations.definition: A shorter air column gives a higher pitch. A tighter, smaller or lighter skin gives a higher pitch.
explanations.description: In a wind instrument, the air inside the tube vibrates. A short air column vibrates faster than a long one. In the Filling Bottle, the note of the pouring water rises as the air column above the water gets shorter. A bansuri player changes the length of the air column with her fingers. Opening a hole lets the air column end at that hole. The column is shorter, so the note is higher. In a drum, a tight skin vibrates. A tighter skin is pulled back harder and gives a higher pitch. A tabla player taps wooden blocks under the straps with a small hammer to tighten the skin. A bigger skin has more to move and gives a lower pitch. A skin that is damp is looser, so its pitch drops. A kanjira player sprinkles water on the skin to lower the note.
examples: A long bansuri plays lower notes than a short one.
The two ends of a mridangam are different sizes. The bigger skin gives the lower sound.
In hot, dry air a drum skin tightens and its pitch creeps up during a concert.
explanations.art: A bansuri with three holes open and three covered, the air column shaded up to the first open hole, beside a tabla with a small hammer tapping a wooden block under its straps.

explanations.concept: How to make a sound louder
explanations.definition: A sound gets louder in four ways: a bigger vibration, more air pushed, a nearer listener, or energy added by an amplifier.
explanations.description: There are four ways. First, give the vibration more energy: pluck harder, hit harder or blow harder. Second, push more air with the same vibration. A thin string cuts through the air and moves very little of it. Rest the string on a soundboard, such as a wooden box, and the wide board pushes far more air. The board adds no energy. It passes the string's energy to the air faster. Third, send the sound one way. A cone or cupped hands stop the sound spreading out on every side. Fourth, add energy from outside. A microphone turns the sound into a weak electric signal. An amplifier makes the signal stronger, using energy from a battery or the mains. A loudspeaker turns the strong signal back into sound. Only this fourth way puts more energy into the sound than the player gave it.
examples: A veena's hollow body is its soundboard. Without it the strings could hardly be heard.
A nadaswaram ends in a wide bell that sends its sound out into the open air.
A phone lying in an empty steel tumbler sounds louder, because the tumbler sends the sound one way.
explanations.art: Four small pictures: a hand plucking hard, a string resting on a hollow box, a child calling through a paper cone, and a microphone joined to an amplifier and a loudspeaker.

explanations.concept: How to make a sound quieter, and what stays the same
explanations.definition: A sound gets quieter when its energy is absorbed, blocked or spread over more space. Its frequency stays the same all the way.
explanations.description: In the Muffle Test, a phone plays a tune under different covers. A thick towel absorbs sound. The vibration gets in among the threads, rubs against them and ends as a tiny amount of warmth. More layers absorb more. A closed steel dabba blocks sound, because its heavy wall is hard for the air to shake. But a gap one finger wide lets a great deal of sound out. This is why a door left a little open hardly keeps noise out. Distance makes a sound quieter too, because the same energy spreads over more space. Through all of this, the tune stays the same tune. Covers and distance take energy from the sound. They do not change how often the pushes arrive, because every push that leaves the phone still arrives, only weaker. Walls and air do weaken high notes more than low notes. That is why far thunder is a low rumble. The notes that get through still have the frequency they started with. Only a source that is moving towards you or away from you changes the pitch you hear.
examples: A song from the next flat is faint, but you can still sing along in tune with it.
Thick curtains, carpets and cushioned seats absorb sound in a cinema hall.
Earmuffs for airport workers have a hard shell to block sound and soft foam to absorb it.
explanations.art: A phone playing a tune under four folded layers of towel, with large sound lines inside and small ones outside, and the same row of musical notes drawn above both.

explanations.definition: Every instrument has a way to set the pitch of each note. It also has a way to change the volume.
explanations.description: Instruments fall into three main families. In string instruments, strings vibrate. The player sets the pitch with the length and the tension of a string. The strength of the pluck or the bow sets the volume. In wind instruments, an air column vibrates. The player sets the pitch with the length of the column, and the volume with the breath. In percussion instruments, a skin, a pot or a bar is struck. Its pitch is mostly set before the concert, by its size and its tension. The player changes the volume with the strength of each stroke. Some instruments can slide smoothly from one pitch to the next, and some cannot. A veena or a violin can slide, because a finger can stop the string anywhere. A harmonium cannot, because each key has one metal reed with one fixed pitch.
examples: Veena: press a fret for pitch, pluck harder for volume.
Bansuri: open or cover holes for pitch, blow more air for volume.
Mridangam: tighten the straps before playing for pitch, strike harder for volume.
explanations.art: A table with three rows, for a veena, a bansuri and a mridangam, and two columns of small drawings showing how each one changes pitch and how each one changes volume.

explanations.concept: Is loudness in the air or in the listener?
explanations.definition: The strength of a sound can be measured in the air. Loudness is what a listener hears. Scientists describe the link between the two in different ways.
explanations.description: A sound meter measures the strength of a sound in the air. Loudness is what a listener hears. The two do not always agree. In 1933, Harvey Fletcher and Wilden Munson asked listeners to match the loudness of tones of different pitch. A low tone of 100 hertz needed far more energy than a 1,000 hertz tone to sound equally loud. Human ears are most sensitive at about 3,000 hertz. So the same reading on a meter can be loud at one pitch and faint at another. Other animals differ again. A sound of 30,000 hertz can be strong in the air, loud to a dog and silent to you.
examples: Many alarms beep near 3,000 hertz, where human ears are most sensitive.
A dog whistle can read high on a meter that picks up ultrasound, and a human hears nothing.
Sound meters often use a setting called dB(A), which counts low sounds less, as human ears do.

perspectives.explanation: The strength of a sound is a fact about the air. It can be measured in decibels with no listener in the room. Loudness is that strength, as closely as a meter can give it.
Loudness is made by an ear and a brain. It depends on the pitch, on the listener's age and on what kind of animal the listener is. The air only has strength. Loudness begins when someone hears.
A strong low sound can be felt through the floor and in the chest with no hearing at all. So the strength of a sound reaches a body in more than one way. Hearing is only one of them.

explanations.art: A sound meter showing the same number for a low drum and a high whistle, and beside it a child's ear with a small wave for the drum and a large wave for the whistle.

agreed.text: Volume depends on the amplitude of the vibration, and pitch depends on its frequency. The two can be changed separately.
agreed.evidence: In Gentle Pluck, Hard Pluck, a bigger pull on the same string gives a higher reading in decibels. The reading in hertz stays the same. Microphones and sound meters show the same for every instrument.

agreed.text: The frequency of a string doubles when its length is halved. It also doubles when its tension is made four times as great.
agreed.evidence: Vincenzo Galilei, a lute player in Italy, tested strings with hanging weights in about 1589. Marin Mersenne measured and published the full rules in 1636. The Water-Bottle String repeats the test.

agreed.text: Every 10 decibels more is ten times the sound energy, and it sounds about twice as loud to most listeners.
agreed.evidence: The decibel is defined in this way. In the 1930s the American scientist Stanley Stevens asked many listeners to judge when a sound was twice as loud.

agreed.text: Long exposure to sound above about 85 decibels harms hearing, and the harm does not heal.
agreed.evidence: Studies of workers in noisy factories, over many years, show hearing loss that grows with the loudness and the hours. Under a microscope, the hair cells of the inner ear are seen to be damaged. In humans they do not grow back.

agreed.text: Sound keeps its frequency as it travels. The exception is a source or a listener moving towards or away from the other.
agreed.evidence: A tuner reads the same frequency near a steady source, far from it, and through a wall or a towel. In the Muffle Test, the covers lower the reading in decibels, and the tune does not change.

challenging.claim: Hitting a drum harder makes its note higher.
challenging.who: A common belief, and many children's first guess.
challenging.for: A hard stroke does sound sharper and brighter than a soft one. A very hard pluck also pulls a string a little tighter for a moment, so its note starts slightly high.
challenging.against: A tuner shows nearly the same frequency for a soft stroke and a hard one. In Gentle Pluck, Hard Pluck, a pull four times as big gives a louder sound at the same frequency. The brighter sound comes from extra high vibrations mixed in, and the main note stays put.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that a harder hit gives a higher note. It gives the evidence for and against.

challenging.claim: Two singers are twice as loud as one.
challenging.for: Two singers do send out twice the sound energy of one singer.
challenging.against: A sound meter reads only 3 decibels more for two equal voices than for one. To most listeners, a sound is twice as loud when it is 10 decibels more. That takes about ten equal voices.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that doubling the number of voices doubles the loudness. It gives the evidence for and against.

challenging.claim: 'High' and 'low' are the natural words for pitch.
challenging.who: Speakers of English, and of many Indian and European languages.
challenging.for: The words feel natural. Many people raise their chin and eyebrows for a high note. Written music puts high notes higher on the page.
challenging.against: Nothing in a high note is higher up. It has a higher frequency. Speakers of Farsi and Turkish call the same notes 'thin' and 'thick'. The ancient Greeks called them 'sharp' and 'heavy'. In 2013, Sarah Dolscheid and her team tested speakers of Farsi and of Dutch. Each group remembered pitches in the way their own words describe them.
challenging.context: This card is about the words 'high' and 'low' for pitch. It asks whether they describe the sound or only our way of talking about it.

challenging.claim: Bigger animals always have lower voices.
challenging.who: A rule that works most of the time.
challenging.for: A bigger animal usually has longer, heavier vocal folds, and these vibrate more slowly. An elephant rumbles far lower than a mouse squeaks.
challenging.against: There are exceptions. A male koala bellows about as low as an elephant, though he weighs about as much as a small dog. In 2013, Benjamin Charlton and his team found a second, much larger pair of folds higher in his throat. So the size of the vibrating part matters, and it does not always match the size of the body.
challenging.context: This card is about a rule of thumb: that large animals have low voices. It gives a real exception.

challenging.claim: A sound meter tells you how loud a sound is.
challenging.who: Makers of sound meter apps, and most people who use them.
challenging.for: A meter gives one number, in decibels, that anyone can check. Laws about noise need a number of this kind.
challenging.against: A meter measures the strength of the sound in the air. Loudness also depends on the pitch and on the listener. A low hum and a high beep with the same reading do not sound equally loud. A phone's microphone is also rough, and two phones can differ by several decibels.
challenging.context: This card is about sound meters. It asks whether the number on a meter is the same thing as loudness.

big_questions.q: In the Muffle Test, a towel makes the alarm quieter, and the tune stays the same. Where does the missing loudness go?
big_questions.hint: Sound is energy, and energy does not vanish. Think about what the threads of the towel are doing as the sound passes.

big_questions.q: A string gives no note until it is pulled tight. Where is the note before you pluck?
big_questions.hint: In the Water-Bottle String, one string gave many notes. Ask what decides the note: the string, the bottle, the pencils, or all of them together.

big_questions.q: A dog hears a 30,000 hertz whistle clearly, and you hear nothing. Is that whistle loud?
big_questions.hint: A meter that picks up ultrasound gives it a number in decibels. Decide whether 'loud' needs a listener, and which listener.

big_questions.q: One family's festival music is another family's sleepless night. Who should decide how loud is too loud?
big_questions.hint: Think of everyone who hears it: a baby, a person who is ill, a night-shift worker, the birds in the tree. Then think about what a rule in decibels can and cannot settle.

big_questions.q: Light has a frequency too, and we see it as colour. Is pitch the colour of sound?
big_questions.hint: Red light has a lower frequency than violet light. Think about what is alike and what is different. Can you mix pitches the way you mix colours?

big_questions.q: A recording lets you hear a singer who died long ago, at the pitch she sang. What exactly has been kept?
big_questions.hint: The air she moved is long gone. Think about what the recording stores, and what it has to rebuild each time it plays.

story.title: The Kanjira That Climbed
story.note: Yazhini, Nila, Kathir and Sumathi Akka are made up, and so is the hall. 'Akka' is a Tamil word for elder sister, and pupils often use it for a young teacher. These things are real. A kanjira is a small frame drum of South India. It is a ring of jackfruit wood 18 to 23 centimetres wide, with a skin glued across one side. A few small metal discs are set in a slot in the ring. The skin was once the skin of a monitor lizard. Monitor lizards are now protected by law in India, and most makers use goat skin. A kanjira's pitch rises as its skin dries under hot lamps. Players really do wet the inside of the skin with a few drops of water to bring the pitch down.
text: The hall in Madurai had a tin roof, and by six in the evening it was as hot as a dosa pan. Four stage lamps hung low over the mat where the musicians sat.

Yazhini was ten. She held her kanjira on her knee and tried not to look at the two hundred people on the folding chairs. A kanjira is a small drum, a ring of jackwood about as wide as a small plate, with a goat skin glued across one side. This was her first concert without her teacher beside her. Sumathi Akka's bus was stuck behind a temple procession, and she had phoned to say, "Start without me. You know everything you need."
Yazhini was not sure that she did.

In front of her sat Nila, who was sixteen and would sing. To her left sat Kathir, who was twelve, with his violin. Beside Yazhini's knee stood the small brass bowl of water that Sumathi Akka put next to every kanjira player. Yazhini had filled it because that was the rule. Nobody had ever told her what it was for. She had always supposed it was for thirsty drummers.
The first song went well. The kanjira's deep dhum sat just under Nila's voice, the way a floor sits under a dancer.

In the second song something went wrong. The dhum was not so deep any more. It had crept up, a little with every line. By the third song it had climbed so far that it sounded like a steel spoon on a tumbler. It went ting where it should have gone dhum, and it quarrelled with Nila's note. Nila glanced back. A man in the front row frowned.
Kathir leaned over. "You are too high," he whispered. "Play softer."
Yazhini played softer. Now the drum was quiet and too high.
"Harder, then," hissed Kathir.
She struck harder. Now the drum was loud and too high. People in the third row could hear exactly how wrong it was.
"It is broken," Kathir whispered. "The skin has gone bad. Just tap the wood until the end."

Yazhini's ears burned. But a thought had caught hold of her, and she held on to it. Soft or hard, the note had not moved at all. Her hand could make the drum louder. Her hand could make it quieter. Her hand could not make it lower. So whatever had pushed the note up, it was not her playing. It was something about the skin.

She pressed the skin with her thumb. That morning it had given a little, like the seat of a cane chair. Now it was as hard as the wooden rim. She looked up at the lamps. They had been shining on the drum for forty minutes. The skin was as dry as an appalam, and it had pulled itself tight.

Tight. She looked at Kathir's violin. Before the concert he had turned a peg, and the string had stretched tighter, and its note had gone up. Tighter, higher. Was it the same for a skin as for a string? If a tight skin sang high, then a looser skin would sing low. And what loosens a dry skin?
She looked down at the brass bowl. It was not for thirsty drummers. It was for thirsty drums.
Between two lines of the song, she dipped two fingers into the bowl. She rubbed the water over the inside of the skin, where the audience could not see. Then she tried one stroke.
Ting. Nothing had changed. Her stomach turned over.
She kept the beat on the wooden rim and counted ten slow breaths. Then she tried again.
Dhum. It was not all the way down, but it was lower. She wet her fingers once more, and only once. A soaked skin goes slack and dull, like wet newspaper. She waited ten more breaths.
Dhum. The note slid back under Nila's voice and stayed there. Nila did not turn round, but her shoulders came down, and the next line of the song had a smile in it.
Kathir stared at the drum. "How did you mend it?"
"It was never broken," Yazhini whispered. "It was dry. The lamps dried the skin and pulled it tight, and a tight skin sings high. I loosened it."
"With water?"
"With water."

When the last song ended, Sumathi Akka was standing at the back of the hall, dusty from the bus. She had heard the last two songs. She pointed at the brass bowl and raised her eyebrows. Yazhini held up two wet fingers.
Sumathi Akka laughed out loud. "I could have told you what the bowl is for," she said afterwards. "But now you will never forget it. A few drops every twenty minutes under those lamps. Never more."
Kathir looked at his violin. Then he looked at the bowl.
"Do not even think about it," said Yazhini. "You have pegs."
story.epiphany: For the parent: the pitch of a drum skin depends on how tight the skin is. The hot lamps dried the skin and tightened it, so the pitch rose. A few drops of water loosened it, and the pitch came down. Before Yazhini could work this out, she had to notice something else. Playing softer and playing harder changed only the volume. That told her the fault was in the pitch, and pitch is not set by the strength of the stroke.
ask: Yazhini played softer and then harder. Why did neither bring the note down?
The lamps touched nothing on the drum. How did they raise its note?
A violin string is tightened with a peg. What does a kanjira player use to loosen a skin, and why does it work?
What do you think would have happened if Yazhini had poured the whole bowl of water on the skin?

roots.context: In this unit you changed the volume and the pitch of a string, and you muffled a ringing phone. Here we ask which part of a sound you can trust when it reaches you from far away.

deep_truth.truth: In the Muffle Test, four layers of towel made the phone's tune much quieter. Every note of the tune stayed at its own pitch. Towels, walls and distance take away a sound's energy and leave its frequency alone. So pitch brings you news of the thing that made the sound, however far the sound has come.
deep_truth.habit: We treat loudness and pitch as two equal facts about a sound. They are not equally lasting. Loudness is changed by every step, every wall and every ear on the way. Frequency is set once, at the source, and it arrives as it left.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Muffle Test, the sound meter read lower under every cover. The tune could still be hummed along with. In Gentle Pluck, Hard Pluck, the note stayed the same while the sound faded to nothing. A tuner reads the same number of hertz near a steady string and far from it. The one exception is a source that moves towards the listener or away.

three.who_am_i: Your family knows your voice from another room, though only a faint part of it gets there. The loudness is lost on the way. The frequencies that make it your voice arrive as you made them.
three.what_is_life: A female cricket or frog finds a male of her own kind by the frequency of his call. He may be far away and faint among a hundred other calls. Many living beings trust pitch in this way.
three.what_is_this_world: Light keeps its frequency as it travels too. Astronomers read what a star is made of from frequencies of light that left it thousands of years ago. If the star is moving away, the frequencies arrive a little lower, and that tells them its speed.

roots.thread: The Water-Bottle String was one string. With three amounts of water and three lengths, it gave many notes. Nothing was added to the string. Only the way it was held and pulled had changed. Many sages taught that the many things of the world come from one source in a similar way. That is a teaching, and a string cannot prove it. What the string shows is smaller and certain. One string can give many notes. Each note belongs to the string together with the way it is held.

teachings.source: Anguttara Nikaya 6.55, the Sona Sutta (the Buddha's talk with the monk Sona)
teachings.teaching: Sona had been a veena player. The Buddha asked him about his strings. When they were too tight, the veena could not be played well. When they were too loose, it could not be played well either. It played well when the strings were tuned to the right pitch between the two. The Buddha told Sona to tune his own effort in the same way.
teachings.link: The talk rests on the science of this unit: the tension of a string sets its pitch. The Buddha used a fact that every player knew to say something about effort. The fact about strings can be tested. The advice about effort is a teaching.

teachings.source: Bharata, Natya Shastra, chapter 28 (India, about 2,000 years ago)
teachings.teaching: The book describes a test with two veenas tuned exactly alike. One is left as it is. On the other, the strings are loosened a little at a time. The two are compared by ear at each step. In this way a listener learns the smallest steps of pitch, which the book calls shrutis.
teachings.link: This is a fair test. One veena is the control, and one thing is changed on the other: the tension. In the Water-Bottle String you did the same. Water took the place of a peg, and a tuner took the place of a trained ear.

teachings.source: Aristotle, Metaphysics, Book 1, chapter 5, on the followers of Pythagoras (Greece, about 2,350 years ago)
teachings.teaching: Aristotle reports that the followers of Pythagoras found the notes of a scale could be written as numbers. From this they came to think that numbers were the makings of all things. They thought the whole sky was a scale.
teachings.link: Pitch really can be written as a number, the frequency, and you measured it in hertz. The step from 'notes are numbers' to 'everything is number' was a bold guess, and Aristotle himself doubted it. Physics still writes the world in numbers, and nobody is sure why that works so well.

science.text: When a wave passes from one material into another, its frequency stays the same. Its speed changes, and so does the distance between one push and the next.

The frequency that arrives changes only if the source or the listener is moving towards or away from the other. This is called the Doppler effect. Light from far galaxies arrives at lower frequencies because space itself has stretched on the way.
Pitch as you hear it is built by your ear and brain. It uses the place and the timing of signals in the inner ear. How it does this is still being worked out.

other_view.view: Pitch is not the same thing as frequency. Pitch is something a brain makes. An old telephone line carries no frequencies below about 300 hertz. A man's voice at 120 hertz still sounds low on it. The brain rebuilds the low pitch from the higher frequencies that do arrive. So the pitch you hear can be a pitch that never reached your ear. On this view, pitch tells you about your own brain as much as about the source.

practice.title: The far sound
practice.say: Sit still and close your eyes. Listen past the sounds in this room. Find the farthest steady sound you can: a train, a temple bell, a koel, a pressure cooker in another flat. It is very quiet by the time it reaches you. Now hum its note, as softly as you can. The loudness you hear belongs to the journey. The note you are humming was made over there.
practice.kid: Close your eyes and sit still. Find the farthest sound you can hear. It is quiet, because it came a long way. Hum its note very softly. That note was made far away.

ask: A song comes faintly through a wall. Which part of it is still exactly as the singer made it, and which part is not?
A sound meter and your ears can disagree about how loud a sound is. Which one would you trust, and for what?
One string gave many notes in the Water-Bottle String. Does the note belong to the string, to the bottle, or to neither alone?
roots.art: A child sitting cross-legged by an open window with eyes closed, and far away across the rooftops a small temple bell with a thin line of the same musical note running from the bell to the child.

games.title: Two Dials: move the volume and the pitch
games.context: This is a card game about what changes the volume of a sound and what changes its pitch. Each card describes one action. You say which of two dials it turns, and which way. Then you move your markers towards a target sound.

printables.title: 24 action cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: Pluck a veena string harder.
items.b: VOLUME UP. A bigger pull gives a bigger amplitude. The pitch stays the same.

items.f: Stand the pencils of a humming string on an empty wooden box.
items.b: VOLUME UP. The box is a soundboard and pushes more air.

items.f: Walk five steps closer to a singer.
items.b: VOLUME UP. Less of the sound has spread away before it reaches you.

items.f: Speak through a paper cone that points at the listener.
items.b: VOLUME UP. The cone sends more of the sound one way.

items.f: Hit a drum harder with the same stick.
items.b: VOLUME UP. The skin moves further. The pitch stays the same.

items.f: Turn up the knob on an amplifier.
items.b: VOLUME UP. The amplifier adds energy from the mains.

items.f: Wrap a ringing phone in four layers of towel.
items.b: VOLUME DOWN. The towel absorbs sound. The tune keeps its pitch.

items.f: Walk ten steps away from a radio.
items.b: VOLUME DOWN. The sound spreads over more space.

items.f: Shut the door between you and the mixie.
items.b: VOLUME DOWN. The door blocks most of the sound.

items.f: Pluck a string more gently.
items.b: VOLUME DOWN. A smaller pull gives a smaller amplitude.

items.f: Put a ticking clock inside a closed steel dabba.
items.b: VOLUME DOWN. The heavy wall blocks the sound.

items.f: Blow a whistle with less air.
items.b: VOLUME DOWN. The air inside vibrates less strongly.

items.f: Turn a peg to make a string tighter.
items.b: PITCH UP. A tighter string is pulled back harder and vibrates faster.

items.f: Press a string on a fret, so that the vibrating part is shorter.
items.b: PITCH UP. A shorter string vibrates faster.

items.f: Change a string for a thinner one, pulled just as tight.
items.b: PITCH UP. A lighter string vibrates faster.

items.f: Open one more hole on a bansuri, so that the air column is shorter.
items.b: PITCH UP. A shorter air column vibrates faster.

items.f: Pour more water into a bottle. Then blow across its mouth.
items.b: PITCH UP. The air column above the water is shorter.

items.f: Leave a damp kanjira under hot lamps until its skin dries.
items.b: PITCH UP. A dry skin pulls tight, and a tight skin vibrates faster.

items.f: Turn a peg to make a string looser.
items.b: PITCH DOWN. A looser string is pulled back less hard.

items.f: Wind copper wire round a string to make it heavier.
items.b: PITCH DOWN. A heavier string vibrates more slowly.

items.f: Cover one more hole on a bansuri, so that the air column is longer.
items.b: PITCH DOWN. A longer air column vibrates more slowly.

items.f: Rub a few drops of water on the skin of a kanjira.
items.b: PITCH DOWN. A damp skin loosens and vibrates more slowly.

items.f: Change a small drum for a bigger one with the same tightness.
items.b: PITCH DOWN. A bigger skin has more to move.

items.f: Slide a pencil so that more of a string is free to vibrate.
items.b: PITCH DOWN. A longer string vibrates more slowly.

rules: Each player has a board with two tracks of seven squares, one for volume and one for pitch. Put a coin on square 4 of each track.
Shuffle the four target cards. Each player takes one and lays it face up. Your goal is the two numbers on your target card.
Shuffle the 24 action cards into a pile, action side up. Lay the top three cards in a row beside the pile, action side up.
On your turn, choose one of the three cards. Read the action aloud. Say which dial it turns and which way: volume up, volume down, pitch up or pitch down.
Turn the card over. If you were right, you may move your coin one square on that track. If you were wrong, you do not move.
A coin cannot go below square 1 or above square 7. Put the used card on a discard pile, and fill the gap in the row from the main pile.
When the main pile runs out, shuffle the discard pile and use it again.
The first player with both coins on the numbers of their target card wins. Playing alone, count your turns and try to finish in ten or fewer.

Each player puts a coin on square 4 of each track and takes a target card. 4. Shuffle the action cards and lay three in a row.
flow.say: Every sound has a volume and a pitch. Your target card names a sound. You must move your two coins until they match it.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Take a board and two coins. Put a coin on each number 4. Take a target card.
flow.context: This is the first step of Two Dials. You set out a board with a volume track and a pitch track, and take a target card.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. 2. On each turn, choose one of the three action cards and read it aloud. 3. Say which dial it turns, and which way. 4. Turn the card over to check. 5. Move a coin one square if you were right. 6. Refill the row.

flow.kid: Choose a card. Say which dial it turns, and which way. Turn it over. Move a coin if you were right.

ask.q: A card says 'Hit a drum harder'. Why does the pitch coin not move?
good: A harder hit changes the amplitude, and that changes only the volume.
The skin is just as tight as before, so it vibrates just as fast.

flow.parent: If a player is unsure, ask what the action changes: the size of the vibration or the number of vibrations each second. A player may choose a card that does not help them, just to answer it.
flow.context: This is the main part of Two Dials. On each turn you choose an action card and say whether it changes the volume or the pitch.

flow.do: 1. Play until one player has both coins on their target numbers. 2. Ask the question below. 3. If there is time, swap target cards and play again.
flow.say: You reached your target. Which cards did you need most? Was there a card that could have moved both coins at once?
flow.kid: Play until someone reaches their target. Which cards did you need most?

ask.q: Did any card move both the volume and the pitch?
good: No. Each action changed only one.
Volume and pitch are changed by different things.

flow.parent: No card moves both dials. That is the point of the game: the things that set volume are different from the things that set pitch.
flow.context: This is the last step of Two Dials. You finish the game and say which actions moved the volume and which moved the pitch.

games.title: Hertz Line: put eighteen sounds in order of frequency
games.context: This is a card game about frequency. Each card names a sound, and its frequency in hertz is on the back. Players build one line of cards, from the lowest frequency to the highest.

rules: Shuffle the 18 cards, sound side up. Deal four cards to each player. Players keep their cards on the table, sound side up, and do not look at the backs.
Put the rest in a pile, sound side up. Take the top card of the pile, turn it over and lay it in the middle. This starts the line.
On your turn, choose one of your cards. Lay it in the line where you think it belongs: lower frequencies to the left, higher to the right.
Say why you chose that place. Then turn your card over and read the frequency.
If the card is in the right place, it stays in the line, number side up.
If it is in the wrong place, move it to its right place in the line. Then take a new card from the pile.
The first player with no cards left wins. If the pile runs out first, the player with the fewest cards wins.
Playing alone, lay all 18 cards in a line, sound side up. Then turn them over and count how many you must move.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 18 cards. 2. Shuffle them, sound side up, and deal four to each player. 3. Turn over the top card of the pile to start the line.
flow.say: Each card is a sound. Its frequency in hertz is hidden on the back. We will build a line from the lowest frequency to the highest.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Take four each. Do not look at the backs. Turn one card over to start.
flow.context: This is the first step of Hertz Line. You deal out sound cards with hidden frequencies and start a line with one card.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. 2. Lay one of your cards in the line and say why it goes there. 3. Turn it over. 4. If it is wrong, move it to its right place and take a new card.
flow.say: Before you place a card, think about what is vibrating. Is it big or small? Long or short? Heavy or light? Big, long and heavy things vibrate slowly.
flow.kid: Lay a card in the line. Say why it goes there. Turn it over and check.

ask.q: A dog hears up to about 45,000 hertz, and you hear up to about 20,000. What does that mean for a dog whistle?
good: A dog can hear a whistle that is silent to me.
The whistle's frequency is above my range and inside the dog's.

flow.parent: The numbers are rounded, and living voices vary a great deal. Cards with close numbers are hard to order. The cat's purr and the lowest sound a person hears are one such pair. Praise a good reason even when the place is wrong.
flow.context: This is the main part of Hertz Line. You take turns to lay sound cards in a line, from the lowest frequency to the highest.

flow.do: 1. When the game ends, look at the whole line. 2. Find the two cards that mark the range of human hearing. 3. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Look at the finished line. Find 20 hertz and 20,000 hertz. Everything between them, a young person can hear. Which sounds lie outside?
flow.kid: Look at the whole line. Find 20 hertz and 20,000 hertz. Which sounds are outside them?

ask.q: Which sounds on the cards are outside human hearing?
good: The elephant's rumble, which is below 20 hertz.
The highest sounds that dogs, cats, bats and dolphins hear, above 20,000 hertz.

flow.parent: Sounds below 20 hertz are called infrasound, and sounds above 20,000 hertz are called ultrasound. Other animals live with sounds that humans miss.
flow.context: This is the last step of Hertz Line. You look at the finished line of frequencies and find which sounds humans cannot hear.

experiments.title: The Water-Bottle String: does twice the pull give twice the frequency?
experiments.context: In this experiment you stretch one string across a table and hang a bottle of water from its end. You change the amount of water, then the length of the string, then its thickness. Each time you measure the note with a tuner app.
experiments.question: How does the pull on a string change its pitch? Does twice the pull give twice the frequency? What do a shorter string and a thicker string do?
experiments.predict: Guess first. The bottle will hang a quarter full, then half full, then full. Will the note go up or down? Will the full bottle give four times the frequency of the quarter-full bottle? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: In the first test, change only the amount of water. That is the independent variable. Keep the same string, the same 40 centimetres between the pencils, and pluck at the middle each time. These are the control variables. Measure the frequency in hertz. That is the dependent variable. Pluck three times for each amount of water, because one reading can be a fluke. In the second test, keep the water the same and change only the length. In the third test, change only the thickness.

materials.item: thin, strong string that hardly stretches: nylon thread, fishing line, kite string with no glass coating, or dental floss. Sewing thread will snap
a table with a leg you can tie the string to, or a table beside a window grille
a 1-litre plastic bottle with its cap, and water
a small cloth bag or plastic carry bag with two handles
four tumblers, mugs or bowls of the same size, each big enough to hold a quarter of the bottle
pencils with round sides
a smooth round pen and sticky tape
a ruler of 30 cm or a measuring tape
a folded towel for the floor under the bottle
a phone with a free tuner app, of the kind used to tune a guitar. It shows the frequency of a note in hertz

experiments.safety: Hang the bottle no more than 10 centimetres above a folded towel on the floor. Keep feet away from under it. If the string snaps, the bottle then falls only a short way.
experiments.record: Draw a table with six rows. Three rows are for the water: a quarter full, half full and full. Two rows are for the lengths of 30 cm and 20 cm. The last row is for the double string. Write three readings in hertz in each row, and circle the middle one.

schedule.what: Build the Water-Bottle String. Measure its note with three amounts of water, three lengths and two thicknesses.

Tie the free end to both handles of the bag. The bag should hang about 10 cm above the floor. 5. Put the folded towel under the bag. 6. Slide the two pencils under the string, 40 cm apart.
