flow.kid: Tie the string to a table leg. Run it across the table. Hang the bag from the other end. Put two pencils under the string.
flow.parent: A grown-up ties the knots and checks that they hold. The pen stops the table edge from cutting or gripping the string. A wooden table works best, because the table top acts as a soundboard. On a stone or glass table, stand the pencils on a large empty cardboard box.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Water-Bottle String. You stretch a string across a table and hang a bag from its end.

flow.do: 1. Fill the bottle to the top. Pour it out equally into the four tumblers. Each tumbler now holds a quarter of the bottle. 2. Pour one tumbler back. The bottle is a quarter full. 3. Put the bottle in the bag and pluck the string once. 4. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write both down.
flow.say: This bottle is a quarter full. Later it will be half full, and then full. Will the note go up or down? Will the full bottle give four times the frequency? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: The bottle is a quarter full. Later it will be full. Will the note go up or down? By how much? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: More water pulls the string tighter, so it should go up.
Four times the water should give four times the frequency.
A tight rubber band sounds higher than a loose one.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children expect four times the water to give four times the frequency. The test will answer it.
flow.context: This step of the Water-Bottle String is for guessing. You guess how more water in the hanging bottle will change the note of the string.

flow.do: 1. Open the tuner app and lay the phone 5 cm from the string. 2. Lift the bag a little and lower it gently, so that the string settles. 3. Pluck the middle of the string gently, three times. Write the three readings. 4. Lift the bottle out, pour in a second tumbler, and put it back. It is now half full. Measure again. 5. Pour in the last two tumblers, so that it is full. Measure again.
flow.say: Pluck gently at the middle and let the phone listen. Read me the number in hertz. Now we add water. Listen first, before you look. Did the note go up or down?
flow.kid: Pluck the middle of the string gently. Read the number in hertz. Add water and do it again.
flow.parent: The note is soft, so make the room quiet and switch off the fan for these minutes. Expect the readings to rise with each amount of water, by smaller steps than the water does. If the number jumps to about double, the app has caught a higher part of the sound. Pluck more gently, at the exact middle. Without an app, listen and hum each note, and put the three in order from lowest to highest.

check.q: In the Water-Bottle String, the water goes from a quarter bottle to a full bottle. What happens to the frequency?
options: It becomes four times as high
check.why: Four times the pull gives about twice the frequency. Twice the pull gives only about 1.4 times the frequency. If you chose four times, you expected the frequency to grow in step with the pull. Look at your own three readings and compare them.

flow.context: In this step of the Water-Bottle String you measure the note three times. The bottle is a quarter full, then half full, then full.

flow.do: 1. Pour water out until the bottle is half full again. Pluck and check the reading. 2. Slide one pencil until the pencils are 30 cm apart. Pluck three times and write the readings. 3. Slide it again to 20 cm apart. Pluck three times and write the readings.
flow.say: Now the water stays the same, and we change only the length. First guess. Will a shorter string sound higher or lower? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Keep the bottle half full. Move one pencil closer. Guess first: higher or lower? Then pluck and read.

ask.q: The string went from 40 cm to 20 cm. What happened to the frequency?
good: It about doubled.
Half the length gave about twice the hertz.

flow.parent: Halving the length should about double the frequency. The pull has not changed, because the same bottle hangs from the string.
flow.context: In this step of the Water-Bottle String you keep the bottle half full. You make the vibrating part of the string shorter and measure the note.

flow.do: 1. Slide the pencils back to 40 cm apart. 2. Cut a second piece of string as long as the table is wide. 3. Wind it round the first string, about ten turns between the pencils. Tape its two ends to the table. 4. Pluck the wound string three times and write the readings.
flow.say: Now the water and the length stay the same. The string is twice as heavy between the pencils. Guess first. Will the note be higher or lower? Why?
flow.kid: Wind a second string round the first. Now it is heavier. Guess: higher or lower? Then pluck and read.
flow.parent: A grown-up cuts the string. The second strand carries none of the pull. It only adds weight. Expect a clearly lower note. If the wound string buzzes, wind it more closely and press the tape down.
flow.context: In this step of the Water-Bottle String you wind a second strand round the string to make it heavier. You measure the note again.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table together. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they measured, and why they think it happened. 3. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at your table. Say what you thought would happen, what you measured, and why you think it happened. Which three changes made the note higher?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you measured. Say why you think it happened.

ask.q: Which three changes made the string's note higher?
good: More water, which means more tension.
A shorter length between the pencils.
One strand in place of two, which means a lighter string.

ask.q: Did twice the water give twice the frequency?
good: No. It gave only about 1.4 times the frequency.
It took four times the water to double the frequency.

flow.parent: A tighter string is pulled back to its rest position harder, so each trip is quicker. A shorter string has less far to go and less of itself to move. A heavier string has more to move, so each trip is slower. The rule for tension is surprising: four times the pull doubles the frequency. Marin Mersenne published these rules in France in 1636. Your numbers will not match the example table. The bag and the bottle also add a little weight of their own. Look for the pattern.
flow.think: A veena has thick strings and thin strings of the same length. Which ones play the low notes, and why?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Water-Bottle String. You say what your table shows about tension, length and thickness.

experiments.title: Gentle Pluck, Hard Pluck: does a bigger vibration change the note?
experiments.context: This experiment uses the Water-Bottle String: a string stretched across a table, with a half-full bottle hanging from its end. You pull the string aside by three measured distances and let go. You measure the loudness and the note each time.
experiments.question: When a string is pulled further aside and let go, what changes: the volume, the pitch, or both?
experiments.predict: Guess first. You will pull the string aside by half a centimetre, 1 centimetre and 2 centimetres. Which pull will be loudest? Will the note be higher, lower or the same? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Change only how far you pull the string aside. That is the independent variable. Keep the same string, the same half-full bottle and the same 40 centimetres between the pencils. Keep the phone in the same place. Measure two things, one at a time: the loudness in decibels and the frequency in hertz. Do each pull three times.
results_table: How far the string was pulled aside
How long the note could be heard (seconds)

materials.item: the Water-Bottle String from the first experiment, with the bottle half full and the pencils 40 cm apart
a ruler
a phone with a free sound meter app and a free tuner app
a stopwatch, or a second person counting seconds

experiments.record: Draw a table with three rows, for pulls of half a centimetre, 1 centimetre and 2 centimetres. For each pull, write the loudness in decibels, the frequency in hertz and the seconds the note lasted.

schedule.what: Pull the Water-Bottle String aside by three measured distances. Measure the loudness and the note each time.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
example_chart.note: These results are made up, to show what a finished table can look like. Write down what you really measure.

setup.art: A ruler lying flat on a table under the middle of a stretched string, crossing it at a right angle, with the string at the zero mark.
setup.caption: 1. Lay a ruler under the middle of the string, across it.

setup.art: A finger pulling the string sideways along the ruler to the 2 cm mark.
setup.caption: 2. Pull the string aside to a mark on the ruler. Let go.

setup.art: A phone lying 10 cm from the string, its screen showing a sound meter dial at 60 dB.
setup.caption: 3. Read the loudness. Then do it again and read the frequency.

flow.do: 1. Check that the bottle is half full and the pencils are 40 cm apart. 2. Lay the ruler flat on the table under the middle of the string, across it. The string should lie over the zero mark. 3. Put the phone 10 cm from the string and open the sound meter. 4. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write both down.
flow.say: You will pull the string aside by half a centimetre, then 1, then 2. Which will be loudest? Will the note change? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: You will pull the string a little, then more. Which pull is loudest? Will the note change? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: A bigger pull gives the string more energy, so it will be louder.
A hard pluck sounds sharper, so the note might be higher.
The string is the same, so the note should be the same.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children, and many adults, expect a harder pluck to give a higher note.
flow.context: This is the first step of Gentle Pluck, Hard Pluck. You set a ruler under the Water-Bottle String and guess what a bigger pull will change.

flow.do: 1. Pull the middle of the string sideways to the half-centimetre mark and let go. 2. Read the highest number on the sound meter. Do this three times. 3. Do the same for 1 cm and for 2 cm. 4. Each time, count the seconds until you cannot hear the note.
flow.say: Pull to the mark, let go, and watch the meter. Tell me the highest number it reaches. Look at the string too. How wide is the blur?
flow.kid: Pull the string to the mark. Let go. Read the highest number. Count how long you hear it.
flow.parent: Keep the room quiet. The readings should rise by roughly 6 decibels each time the pull doubles. Phone microphones are rough, so look at the order and not at the exact numbers. Without an app, a listener one metre away gives each pluck a score of 1, 2 or 3.
flow.context: In this step of Gentle Pluck, Hard Pluck you pull the Water-Bottle String aside by three distances. You measure the loudness of each in decibels.

flow.do: 1. Open the tuner app in place of the sound meter. 2. Pull the string to the half-centimetre mark, let go and read the frequency. 3. Do the same for 1 cm and 2 cm. 4. After the 2 cm pull, keep watching the number as the sound dies away.
flow.say: Now the tuner. Same three pulls. Read me the hertz each time. After the biggest pull, keep watching as the sound fades. Does the number fall?
flow.kid: Now use the tuner. Do the same three pulls. Read the hertz. Watch the number as the sound fades.
flow.parent: The three readings should be nearly the same, within a few hertz. The biggest pull may read a little high for the first instant, because the pull stretches the string tighter. As the sound fades, the number stays steady until the app loses the sound.

check.q: In Gentle Pluck, Hard Pluck, the pull on the string goes from half a centimetre to 2 centimetres. What changes?
options: Volume goes up. Pitch stays the same.
Pitch goes up. Volume stays the same.
check.why: A bigger pull gives a bigger amplitude, and that gives a louder sound. The frequency is set by the string's tension, length and weight, and none of those changed. If you chose a higher pitch, compare your three readings in hertz.

flow.context: In this step of Gentle Pluck, Hard Pluck you make the same three pulls on the Water-Bottle String. This time you measure the frequency.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table together. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they measured, and why they think it happened. 3. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at your table. Say what you thought would happen, what you measured, and why you think it happened. What does a harder pluck change?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you measured. Say why you think it happened.

ask.q: As the sound faded, the blur got narrower. What happened to the note?
good: It stayed the same.
It got quieter, and it did not get lower.

flow.parent: Your finger does more work to pull the string further. So the string starts with more energy and a bigger amplitude. It pushes the air harder, and the sound is louder. The frequency does not change. The string makes wider trips in the same time, by moving faster. So volume comes from amplitude, and pitch comes from frequency. As the sound dies, the string loses amplitude and keeps its frequency.
flow.think: A singer holds one note and lets it fade away. What is her voice box changing, and what is it keeping the same?
flow.context: This is the last step of Gentle Pluck, Hard Pluck. You say what a bigger pull on the Water-Bottle String changed, and what it left the same.

experiments.title: The Muffle Test: what makes a ringing phone quietest?
experiments.context: In this experiment a phone plays the same tune under five different covers. A second phone measures the volume from 50 centimetres away. You find which cover muffles best, and you listen for any change in the tune.
experiments.question: Which cover makes a ringing phone quietest: one layer of towel, four layers, or a closed steel dabba? What does a small gap do? Does any cover change the pitch of the tune?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Put the five covers in order, from the loudest reading to the quietest. Will any cover make the tune sound lower or higher? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Change only the cover. That is the independent variable. Use the same phone, the same tune from its start, and the same volume setting, at about half. Keep both phones on the same marks, 50 centimetres apart. Measure the highest reading in decibels in 10 seconds. That is the dependent variable. Test each cover twice. Keep the room as quiet as you can for every test.
results_table: Did the tune keep its pitch?

materials.item: a phone that can play an alarm tune or a song
a second phone with a free sound meter app
a cotton bath towel
a steel dabba with a lid, big enough to hold the phone
a ruler or measuring tape
sticky tape or chalk to mark where the phones go

experiments.record: Draw a table with five rows. The first three are for no cover, one layer of towel and four layers of towel. The last two are for the closed dabba, and the dabba with its lid open by one finger-width. Write two readings in decibels for each. In the last column write yes or no: did the tune keep its pitch?

schedule.what: Play one tune on a phone under five covers. Measure the volume each time from 50 cm away, and listen to the pitch of the tune.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
cols: Did the tune keep its pitch?
rows: Dabba with the lid open one finger-width
example_chart.note: These results are made up, to show what a finished table can look like. Write down what you really measure.

setup.art: A phone lying on a folded towel on a table, and a second phone on a book 50 cm away, with a ruler between them and tape marks under both.
setup.caption: 1. Put the ringing phone on a folded towel. Put the meter phone 50 cm away. Mark both places.

setup.art: The first phone covered by a towel folded into four layers, with small sound lines coming out.
setup.caption: 2. Cover the phone: one layer of towel, then four layers.

setup.art: The first phone inside a steel dabba whose lid is lifted by one finger-width, with sound lines escaping through the gap.
setup.caption: 3. Put the phone in a steel dabba. Close the lid. Then open it by one finger-width.

setup.art: The second phone showing a sound meter dial, with a child writing the number in a table.
setup.caption: 4. Each time, write the highest reading in 10 seconds.

flow.do: 1. Fold one towel and lay it on the table. Put the first phone on it. 2. Choose an alarm tune or a song and set the volume to about half. 3. Put the second phone on a book 50 cm away and open the sound meter. 4. Mark both places with tape. 5. Play the tune for 10 seconds with no cover. Write the highest reading. Do it twice.
flow.say: This phone will play the same tune every time, from the start. The other phone will measure it. First we measure it with no cover at all.
flow.kid: Put the phone on a folded towel. Play the tune. Read the highest number on the other phone.
flow.parent: The folded towel under the phone stops the table acting as a soundboard. Half volume is enough. Nobody needs to put an ear near the phone. Without a sound meter app, walk away from the phone until you cannot hear the tune, and count your steps.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Muffle Test. You set up a ringing phone and a meter phone 50 cm apart, and measure the tune with no cover.

flow.do: 1. Show the covers: one towel, the same towel folded into four layers, and the steel dabba. 2. Say that the dabba will be tested closed, and then with its lid open by one finger-width. 3. Ask for an order, from loudest to quietest, and a reason. Write both down.
flow.say: Here are the covers. Put them in order, from the loudest reading to the quietest. Will any of them change the tune itself? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the covers. Which will be loudest? Which will be quietest? Will the tune change? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: More layers should soak up more sound.
Steel is hard, so sound might bounce around inside and come out.
The gap will let sound out.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. The order of the towel and the dabba is not obvious, and homes differ.
flow.context: This step of the Muffle Test is for guessing. You put five covers for a ringing phone in order, from the loudest reading to the quietest.

flow.do: 1. Lay the second towel over the phone in one layer. Play the tune for 10 seconds and write the highest reading. Do it twice. 2. Fold that towel into four layers and cover the phone again. Measure twice. 3. Each time, listen to the tune. Hum along with it.
flow.say: One layer first, then four. Watch the meter. Then listen to the tune itself. Can you still hum along? Is it the same tune, at the same pitch?
flow.kid: Cover the phone with one layer. Read the number. Now fold the towel into four. Read again. Hum along.
flow.parent: Expect a small drop for one layer and a bigger drop for four. The tune sounds duller, because cloth takes more from high notes than from low notes. Every note that gets through is still at its own pitch, so your child can hum along in tune.
flow.context: In this step of the Muffle Test you cover the ringing phone with one layer of towel. Then you cover it with four layers. You measure the volume each time.

flow.do: 1. Take the towel off. Put the phone inside the dabba, on a small folded cloth, and close the lid. Measure twice. 2. Lift one side of the lid by one finger-width and rest it there. Measure twice. 3. Listen to the tune each time.
flow.say: Now the steel dabba, closed. Read the meter. Now I open the lid by the width of one finger. Guess first. Will the reading change a little or a lot?
flow.kid: Put the phone in the dabba. Close the lid. Read the number. Open the lid a little. Read again.
flow.parent: A closed dabba usually gives a low reading, because its heavy wall is hard for the air to shake. A narrow gap lets a lot of the sound back out. If your dabba gives a higher reading than the towels, write that down. A thin or rattling lid can pass sound on.

check.q: In the Muffle Test, the lid of the steel dabba is opened by one finger-width. What happens to the reading?
check.why: Sound gets out through any gap, however narrow. That is why a door left a little open keeps out very little noise. If you chose 'almost the same', you judged the gap by its size. Look at your own two readings.

flow.context: In this step of the Muffle Test you put the ringing phone in a closed steel dabba. Then you open the lid by one finger-width and measure again.

flow.do: 1. Take the phone out and play the tune with no cover. 2. Your child walks to the next room, or as far away as the home allows, and listens. 3. They hum the tune there, then walk back still humming.
flow.say: Walk to the next room and listen. Is the tune quieter? Is it still the same tune? Hum it there, and keep humming as you walk back.
flow.kid: Walk to the next room. Is the tune quieter? Hum it. Walk back, still humming. Does your hum still fit?
flow.parent: The tune is fainter in the next room, and the hum still fits when your child comes back. Distance and walls lower the volume. They do not change the frequency of any note.
flow.context: In this step of the Muffle Test the phone plays with no cover. You walk to the next room and check what distance does to the volume and to the pitch.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table together. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they measured, and why they think it happened. 3. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at your table. Say what you thought would happen, what you measured, and why you think it happened. Which cover was best? What did no cover change?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you measured. Say why you think it happened.

ask.q: What did every cover change, and what did no cover change?
good: Every cover made the tune quieter.
No cover changed the pitch of the tune.

ask.q: Where did the missing sound energy go?
good: Into the towel, as a tiny amount of warmth.
Some bounced back inside the dabba.

flow.parent: A thick towel absorbs sound. The vibration gets in among the threads, rubs against them, and ends as a tiny amount of warmth. More layers absorb more. A steel wall blocks sound, because it is heavy and hard to shake, but any gap lets sound through. None of this changes the frequency. Every push that leaves the phone still arrives, only weaker, so the pushes arrive just as often. This is why you know a song through a wall.
flow.think: A friend calls your name from far away. What tells you who it is: the loudness of the call, or something else?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Muffle Test. You say which cover made the ringing phone quietest, and what none of the covers changed.

activities.title: Four Hums: can you change loudness and pitch separately?
activities.context: This is a short activity to start the unit. You hum in four ways with a hand on your throat. Then you sort the sounds of your home into four boxes.

materials.item: your own voice
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Hum soft and low, strong and low, soft and high, strong and high. Then sort eight home sounds into four boxes.

activities.record: Draw a square and divide it into four boxes: quiet and low, loud and low, quiet and high, loud and high. Write two sounds from your home in each box.

setup.art: A child sitting with one hand resting lightly on the front of her throat, humming with closed lips.
setup.caption: 1. Rest a hand on your throat. Hum a low note softly, then strongly.

setup.art: The same child humming with her eyebrows raised and a small high note above her head.
setup.caption: 2. Hum a high note softly, then strongly.

setup.art: A square on paper divided into four boxes labelled quiet and low, loud and low, quiet and high, loud and high.
setup.caption: 3. Draw four boxes. Write two home sounds in each.

flow.do: 1. Your child rests one hand lightly on the front of their throat. 2. They hum a low note softly, then the same note strongly. 3. They hum a high note softly, then the same note strongly. A strong hum is enough. Nobody needs to shout.
flow.say: Hum a low note softly. Now the same note, stronger. Now a high note softly, and then stronger. What do you notice in your throat? What do you wonder?
flow.kid: Put a hand on your throat. Hum low and soft. Then low and strong. Then high and soft. Then high and strong.

ask.q: What changed when the hum got stronger? What changed when it got higher?
good: The buzz under my hand got bigger when it was stronger.
Something in my throat tightened or moved up when it was higher.
I could change one without the other.

flow.parent: Do not explain yet. Write down what your child notices and wonders. Most children feel a bigger buzz for the strong hum and a tightening or a lift for the high hum.
flow.context: This is the first step of Four Hums. You hum a low note and a high note, each softly and then strongly, and feel your throat.

flow.do: 1. Draw a square and divide it into four boxes. 2. Label them: quiet and low, loud and low, quiet and high, loud and high. 3. Together, think of eight sounds in your home and street. 4. Your child writes each one in a box.
flow.say: Here are four boxes. Where does the fridge's hum go? The doorbell? A crow? A spoon dropped on the floor? Find two sounds for every box.
flow.kid: Draw four boxes. Think of eight sounds at home. Write each one in the box where it fits.
flow.parent: There is no single right box for some sounds, and the talk matters more than the answer. A fridge is quiet and low. A mixie is loud. A sparrow is quiet and high. If a box stays empty, listen at the window for a minute.
flow.context: In this step of Four Hums you sort eight sounds from your home into four boxes: quiet or loud, and low or high.

flow.do: 1. Ask the question below. 2. Take any answer, and write it down to look at again later.
flow.say: You made a hum louder without making it higher. You made it higher without making it louder. So are loud and high the same thing? What might each one be?
flow.kid: You changed loud without changing high. Are loud and high the same thing? What do you think?

ask.q: Are loud and high the same thing?
good: No. I can change one and keep the other.
Loud is how strong it is. High is something else, maybe how fast it shakes.

flow.parent: Any reasoned answer is good. The experiments that follow measure the two things separately.
flow.context: This is the last step of Four Hums. You say whether loudness and pitch are one thing or two.

activities.title: The Sound Grid: eight home sounds, two numbers
activities.context: In this activity you measure the volume of eight sounds in your home with a sound meter app. You judge the pitch of each by ear. Then you place all eight on one grid.

materials.item: a phone with a free sound meter app
a measuring tape or a ruler
squared paper, or plain paper and a ruler
a pencil and a red pencil

activities.safety: Measure every sound from at least 1 metre away, and the mixie from 2 metres. Run the mixie for only 5 seconds. Do not put an ear or the phone close to any loud sound.

schedule.what: Measure eight home sounds in decibels from 1 metre. Judge the pitch of each. Place all eight on a grid.

activities.record: Make a table with four columns: the sound, the reading in decibels, the pitch (low, middle or high), and a guess of what is vibrating. Then draw the grid and put a dot with a name for each sound.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
rows: A tap running into a steel sink
A spoon tapped on a steel tumbler
example_chart.note: These results are made up, to show what a finished table can look like. Write down what you really measure.

setup.art: A child holding a phone at arm's length, 1 metre from a humming fridge, with a measuring tape on the floor between them.
setup.caption: 1. Hold the phone 1 metre from each sound. Read the decibels.

setup.art: A hand-drawn grid with 'low, middle, high' along the bottom and decibels from 20 to 100 up the side, with a red line drawn across at 85.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a grid. Pitch goes along the bottom, and decibels go up the side. Draw a red line at 85.

setup.art: The same grid with eight named dots on it, a fridge low on the left and a doorbell higher on the right.
setup.caption: 3. Put a dot on the grid for each sound.

flow.do: 1. Choose eight sounds in your home, some quiet and some loud. 2. Your child guesses which will be loudest and which quietest, in decibels. 3. Write the guesses down.
flow.say: We will measure eight sounds, each from 1 metre away. Which do you think will give the biggest number? Which the smallest? Why?
flow.kid: Pick eight sounds at home. Guess which is loudest and which is quietest. Say why.
flow.parent: Good quiet choices are a whisper, the fridge, a fan and a running tap. Louder ones are talking, a spoon on a tumbler, the doorbell and the mixie. Leave out any sound that hurts.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Sound Grid. You choose eight sounds in your home and guess which is loudest and which is quietest.

flow.do: 1. Measure 1 metre from the first sound. 2. Hold the phone there and read the highest number in 5 seconds. 3. Your child says the pitch by ear: low, middle or high. 4. Write both in the table. 5. Do the same for all eight. A grown-up runs the mixie for 5 seconds, and you measure it from 2 metres.
flow.say: Hold the phone at the 1 metre mark. What is the number? Now listen to the sound itself. Is its pitch low, middle or high?
flow.kid: Hold the phone 1 metre away. Read the number. Is the pitch low, middle or high? Write both.
flow.parent: Phone meters are rough, and two phones can differ by several decibels. The order of the sounds is what matters. Some sounds, such as a fan, have no clear pitch. Write 'low' if the sound is mostly a deep hum. Write 'high' if it is mostly a hiss or a ring. Without an app, score each sound from 1 for very quiet to 5 for very loud.
flow.context: In this step of the Sound Grid you measure the volume of each of your eight sounds from 1 metre. You judge the pitch of each by ear.

flow.do: 1. Draw a grid. Write low, middle and high along the bottom. 2. Mark decibels up the side, from 20 to 100 in steps of 10. 3. Draw a red line across at 85. 4. Your child puts a dot and a name on the grid for each sound.
flow.say: Each sound gets one dot. Its place along the bottom shows its pitch, and its height shows its volume. Is any dot above the red line?
flow.kid: Draw the grid. Put a dot for each sound. Pitch goes along, and decibels go up.
flow.parent: Sounds above 85 decibels can harm hearing over hours. A mixie is near the line, and it runs for only a minute or two at a time.
flow.context: In this step of the Sound Grid you place your eight sounds on a grid. Pitch runs along the bottom and volume runs up the side.

flow.do: 1. Look at the finished grid together. 2. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Look at your grid. Are the loud sounds all high? Are the quiet sounds all low? What does that tell you about volume and pitch?
flow.kid: Look at your dots. Are loud sounds always high? Are quiet sounds always low?

ask.q: Are the loud sounds all high-pitched?
good: No. The dots are spread over the whole grid.
A sound can be loud and low, or quiet and high.

ask.q: Which sound was 10 decibels more than another? How much more energy does it carry?
good: Ten times as much.

flow.parent: The dots spread over the grid because volume and pitch are separate measures. Knowing one tells you nothing about the other.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Sound Grid. You look at where your eight sounds fell, and say what the grid shows.

activities.title: The Filling Bottle: hear an air column get shorter
activities.context: In this activity you pour water into a tall bottle and listen. The sound of the pouring changes as the bottle fills. You use that change to tell how full the bottle is with your eyes shut.

materials.item: a tall, narrow bottle of about 1 litre
a jug or a mug with a spout, and water
a bucket or a sink to work over
a ruler

schedule.what: Pour water into a tall bottle and listen to the note rise. Then tell by ear, with eyes shut, when the bottle is nearly full.

activities.record: Draw the bottle three times: nearly empty, half full and nearly full. Shade the air column in each. Write its length in centimetres, and write 'lowest', 'middle' or 'highest' note beside it.

setup.art: A tall plastic bottle standing in a sink while a thin stream of water pours into it from a jug.
setup.caption: 1. Pour a thin, steady stream of water into a tall bottle. Listen.

setup.art: A child with eyes shut and one hand raised, beside a parent pouring water into the bottle.
setup.caption: 2. Shut your eyes. Say 'stop' when you think the bottle is three-quarters full.

setup.art: A ruler held beside the bottle, measuring from the water surface up to the mouth of the bottle.
setup.caption: 3. Measure the air column: from the water up to the mouth.

flow.do: 1. Stand the bottle in the sink or the bucket. 2. Pour water in from the jug in a thin, steady stream, until the bottle is full. 3. Your child listens with eyes open. 4. Empty the bottle.
flow.say: Listen to the sound the water makes inside the bottle while I pour. What do you notice? What do you wonder?
flow.kid: Listen while the water pours in. What happens to the sound? What do you wonder?

ask.q: What happened to the sound as the bottle filled?
good: It got higher and higher.
It rose fastest near the end.

flow.parent: The sound rises in pitch as the bottle fills. Keep the stream thin and steady, and aim it at the middle, not down the side. Do not explain yet.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Filling Bottle. You listen to the sound of water pouring into a tall bottle as it fills.

flow.do: 1. Your child shuts their eyes. 2. Pour again in the same steady stream. 3. Your child says 'stop' when they think the bottle is three-quarters full. 4. Measure the height of the water and the height of the bottle with the ruler. 5. Swap places and try again.
flow.say: Now shut your eyes. Say stop when you think the bottle is three-quarters full. Use only your ears. How did you know?
flow.kid: Shut your eyes. Listen to the pouring. Say stop when the bottle is three-quarters full.
flow.parent: Most people get close on the second or third try. You do this every time you fill a water bottle at the tap without looking.
flow.context: In this step of the Filling Bottle you shut your eyes. You use the rising note of the pouring water to tell how full the bottle is.

flow.do: 1. Fill the bottle a quarter full. Measure the air column, from the water up to the mouth. 2. Do the same half full and three-quarters full. 3. Ask the question below before you explain. 4. Then read the note to your child.
flow.say: The water is not what sings. Something else in the bottle is getting shorter as the water rises. What is it? What does a shorter one do to the note?
flow.kid: Measure the air above the water three times. What gets shorter as the bottle fills? What happens to the note?

ask.q: What is getting shorter as the bottle fills?
good: The air above the water.
The air column.

flow.parent: The falling water sets the air column in the bottle vibrating. As the bottle fills, the air column gets shorter. A shorter air column vibrates faster, so the note rises. A bansuri works in the same way: opening a hole makes the air column shorter.
flow.think: A short bansuri and a long bansuri are played with every hole covered. Which gives the lower note?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Filling Bottle. You measure the air column above the water at three levels, and link its length to the note.

activities.title: The Rubber Band Puzzle: three changes at once
activities.context: In this activity you stretch a rubber band further and further and pluck it. The note rises much less than you expect. You work out why, and you see why a fair test changes only one thing.

materials.item: a rubber band about 8 cm long when it lies flat
a door handle or a window grille to hook the band on
a ruler

activities.safety: A stretched rubber band can snap. Hold it away from faces, and do not stretch it past 30 centimetres.

schedule.what: Stretch a rubber band to 15, 22 and 30 cm and pluck it. Then keep the stretch the same and pinch the band in the middle.

activities.record: Write the three lengths, 15 cm, 22 cm and 30 cm. Beside each write whether the note was lower, the same or higher than the one before. Then write what the pinch did.

setup.art: A rubber band hooked over a door handle and pulled out straight by a child's finger, with a ruler held beside it showing 15 cm.
setup.caption: 1. Hook a rubber band on a door handle. Stretch it to 15 cm and pluck it.

setup.art: The same band stretched to 30 cm, looking much thinner, being plucked.
setup.caption: 2. Stretch it to 22 cm, then 30 cm. Pluck each time.

setup.art: The band stretched to 22 cm with a second person's finger and thumb pinching it exactly halfway, and the child plucking one half.
setup.caption: 3. Hold it at 22 cm. A partner pinches the middle. Pluck one half.

flow.do: 1. Hook the band over a door handle. 2. Your child pulls the other end with one finger until the band is 15 cm long, and plucks it. 3. Ask for a guess: what will the note do at 22 cm and at 30 cm? 4. Then they stretch it to 22 cm and 30 cm, and pluck each time.
flow.say: At 30 centimetres this band will be pulled about three times as hard as at 15. What will the note do? Why do you think so? Now try it.
flow.kid: Stretch the band to 15 cm and pluck. Guess what happens at 30 cm. Then try it.

ask.q: What did you expect, and what happened?
good: I expected a much higher note, because it was much tighter.
The note rose only a little.

flow.parent: Most bands rise a little and then stay nearly the same. A few rise more. Either way, the rise is far smaller than the same tightening gives on a string of fixed length. Do not explain yet.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Rubber Band Puzzle. You stretch a rubber band to three lengths and listen to its note each time.

flow.do: 1. Hold the band at 22 cm. 2. A partner pinches the band firmly, exactly halfway along. 3. Your child plucks one half. 4. Let go of the pinch and pluck the whole band again.
flow.say: Now the stretch stays the same. My pinch makes the vibrating part half as long. Guess first. What will the note do?
flow.kid: Keep the band at 22 cm. A partner pinches the middle. Pluck one half. What happens to the note?

ask.q: What did the pinch do to the note?
good: It went up a lot.
Half the length gave a much higher note.

flow.parent: The pinch changes one thing only, the length. The note jumps up clearly. This is a fair test.
flow.context: In this step of the Rubber Band Puzzle the stretch stays the same. A pinch makes the vibrating part of the band half as long.

flow.do: 1. Ask the question below before you explain. 2. Let your child look at the band at 15 cm and at 30 cm. 3. Then read them the note.
flow.say: When you stretched the band, tighter was not the only change. Look at it at 15 centimetres, and again at 30. What else changed?
flow.kid: Look at the band short, then long. Tighter was one change. Find two more.

ask.q: What three things changed when the band was stretched?
good: It got tighter.
It got longer.
It got thinner.

ask.q: Which of those raise the note, and which lowers it?
good: Tighter and thinner raise it.
Longer lowers it.

flow.parent: Stretching changes three things at once. The band gets tighter, which raises the note. It gets thinner, which also raises the note. It gets longer, which lowers the note. The changes nearly cancel. So this test cannot show what tension does. In the Water-Bottle String, only the water changed, and the length stayed at 40 cm. That is why a fair test changes one thing at a time.
flow.think: When you sing a higher note, your vocal folds are stretched longer and tighter. Why does the note go up and not down?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Rubber Band Puzzle. You find the three things that change when a rubber band is stretched.

activities.title: Instrument Detective: how does each instrument change its volume and its pitch?
activities.context: In this activity you choose three instruments, one from each family: string, wind and percussion. For each one you work out what vibrates. You also find how the player changes the pitch and the volume.

materials.item: a real instrument at home if you have one, or a picture or a concert video of each instrument you choose
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Choose a string, a wind and a percussion instrument. Work out how each one changes its pitch and its volume.

activities.record: Make a table with three rows, one for each instrument. Give it three columns: what vibrates, how the player changes the pitch, and how the player changes the volume.

example_chart.title: Answers for eight instruments
rows: Press a string on a fret to shorten it. Pull it sideways to tighten it.
Press a finger on a string to shorten it.
Press the bow harder, or move it faster.
The air column in the tube
Open or cover finger holes to change the length of the air column.
The air column, started by a reed
Blow harder. The wide bell sends the sound out.
Metal reeds, one for each key
Press a different key. Each reed has one pitch.
Tighten or loosen the straps before playing.
Wet the skin to lower it. Press the skin from behind to raise it.
The wall of a clay pot, and the air inside
Choose a pot of the right size. Press the mouth against the belly.
example_chart.note: Look at this table only after you have filled in your own.

setup.art: A veena, a bansuri and a mridangam drawn side by side on a page, each with a blank label line under it.
setup.caption: 1. Choose one string, one wind and one percussion instrument.

setup.art: A child watching a concert video on a phone and pointing at the player's left hand on the neck of a veena.
setup.caption: 2. Watch the player's hands. What changes when the note changes?

setup.art: A hand-drawn table with three rows and three columns, half filled in.
setup.caption: 3. Fill in the table: what vibrates, how pitch changes, how volume changes.

flow.do: 1. Read the list together: veena, violin, bansuri, nadaswaram, harmonium, mridangam, kanjira, ghatam. 2. Your child chooses one string, one wind and one percussion instrument. 3. Find the real instrument, a picture of it, or a concert video.
flow.say: Choose three instruments, one from each family. In a string instrument, strings vibrate. In a wind instrument, air vibrates. A percussion instrument is struck.
flow.kid: Pick three instruments: one with strings, one you blow, one you strike. Find a picture or a video.
flow.parent: A harmonium is a wind instrument, because air from its bellows makes its metal reeds vibrate. Search for a concert clip by the instrument's name. Watch it first yourself.
flow.context: This is the first step of Instrument Detective. You choose a string instrument, a wind instrument and a percussion instrument to study.

flow.do: 1. Your child looks at each instrument or watches it being played for two minutes. 2. For each one they answer three questions and fill in a row of the table. 3. Do not show the answer table yet.
flow.say: Watch the player's hands. What is vibrating? What does the player do to get a higher note? What does the player do to get a louder note?
flow.kid: Watch the player's hands. What vibrates? How does the note go higher? How does it get louder?

ask.q: What does the player do to get a higher note?
good: Makes the string shorter with a finger.
Opens a hole, so that the air column is shorter.
A drum's note is set before playing, by tightening the skin.

flow.parent: Use what the Water-Bottle String and the Filling Bottle showed. A shorter or tighter string is higher. A shorter air column is higher. A tighter skin is higher.
flow.context: In this step of Instrument Detective you study your three instruments. For each one you find what vibrates and how its pitch and volume are changed.

flow.do: 1. Open the answer table. 2. Your child compares their three rows with it. 3. Talk about any row that differs.
flow.say: Now compare your table with this one. Where do you agree? Where is yours different? Could both be right?
flow.kid: Look at the answer table. Check your three rows. What did you find that the table missed?
flow.parent: A child often notices things the table leaves out, such as a violin player's shaking finger. Give credit for what they saw.
flow.context: In this step of Instrument Detective you compare your own table for three instruments with a filled-in table for eight.

flow.do: 1. Ask the question below. 2. Let your child test the answer by humming a slide from a low note to a high note.
flow.say: Some instruments can slide smoothly from one note to the next, and some cannot. Which of your three can slide? What lets them do it?
flow.kid: Which of your instruments can slide from one note to the next? Why can they?

ask.q: Which instruments can slide between notes, and why?
good: A veena or a violin can, because a finger can stop the string anywhere.
A harmonium cannot, because each reed has one pitch.
A voice can, because the vocal folds can tighten smoothly.

flow.parent: Sliding needs a pitch control that changes smoothly: the length or the tension of a string, or the tightness of the vocal folds. A bansuri player slides by uncovering a hole a little at a time.
flow.context: This is the last step of Instrument Detective. You work out which instruments can slide smoothly between notes, and why.

projects.title: Two Instruments, One Tune: match a string to three bottles
projects.context: In this two-day project you tune three bottles of water to three notes by blowing across them. The Water-Bottle String is a string stretched across a table and pulled tight by a hanging bottle. You find the three lengths of it that give the same notes. Then you play one tune on both.

materials.item: bottles of the same size and shape, glass or hard plastic, of 500 ml to 1 litre
water and a jug
the Water-Bottle String from the first experiment, with the bottle half full
strips of paper and sticky tape, for marks
a ruler
a phone with a free tuner app, if you have one

schedule.what: Tune three bottles to three rising notes by adding water and blowing across them. Mark the water levels.
Find the three string lengths that match the bottles. Mark them, measure them, and play a tune on both instruments.

projects.record: For each of the three notes, write two lengths in centimetres: the air column in the bottle, and the string. Write the frequency too, if you have a tuner. Then write the tune you played as a row of numbers, such as 1 2 3 2 1.

setup.art: Three identical bottles in a row with rising levels of water, a strip of tape marking each level, and a child blowing across the mouth of the first.
setup.caption: 1. Day 1: tune three bottles to three rising notes. Mark the water levels.

setup.art: The Water-Bottle String on a table with one pencil being slid along under the string, and three paper marks taped to the table beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Day 2: slide a pencil until the string matches each bottle. Mark each place.

setup.art: A child plucking the string with one hand at the second mark, with the three bottles standing beside the table.
setup.caption: 3. Play the same tune on the bottles and on the string.

flow.do: 1. Stand the three bottles in a row. 2. Your child blows gently across the mouth of an empty one until it hoots. 3. Pour water into the first bottle until it is about a quarter full. This is note 1. 4. Add water to the second until its note is one step higher. This is note 2. 5. Do the same for the third. This is note 3.
flow.say: Blow across the top, as if you were cooling a hot drink. Sing Sa, Re, Ga. Now add water to each bottle until the three bottles sing those three notes.
flow.kid: Blow across each bottle. Add water to change the note. Make three notes that step up.
flow.parent: To make a bottle hoot, rest the lower lip on the rim and blow a thin stream across the opening. More water gives a shorter air column and a higher note. Any three notes that step up will do. With a tuner app, write down each frequency.
flow.context: This is the first step of Two Instruments, One Tune. You tune three bottles to three rising notes by adding water and blowing across them.

flow.do: 1. Mark each water level with tape. 2. Measure each air column, from the water to the mouth, and write it down. 3. Your child plays a short tune on the bottles, such as 1 2 3 2 1. 4. Keep the bottles for the next day.
flow.say: Measure the air column in each bottle. Which bottle has the shortest one? Which gives the highest note? Now play me a tune on the three.
flow.kid: Mark the water levels. Measure the air in each bottle. Play a tune: 1 2 3 2 1.
flow.parent: If water evaporates overnight, top each bottle up to its tape mark the next day.
flow.context: In this step of Two Instruments, One Tune you mark and measure the three tuned bottles. Then you play a short tune on them.

flow.do: 1. Check that the Water-Bottle String has its bottle half full. 2. Your child blows bottle 1, then plucks the string. 3. They slide one pencil until the string's note matches the bottle. 4. Tape a paper mark on the table at the pencil. 5. Do the same for bottles 2 and 3. 6. Measure the three string lengths.
flow.say: Blow the bottle, then pluck the string. Is the string higher or lower than the bottle? Which way must the pencil move to bring them together?
flow.kid: Blow bottle 1. Pluck the string. Slide the pencil until the two notes match. Mark the place.
flow.parent: Matching by ear takes patience. Hum the bottle's note first, then find it on the string. A tuner app helps: move the pencil until the string shows the same number as the bottle. If the string is too low even at 15 cm, hang the full bottle on it.
flow.context: In this step of Two Instruments, One Tune you slide a pencil under the Water-Bottle String on the table. You find the length that matches each of the three tuned bottles.

flow.do: 1. Your child plays the same tune on the bottles and then on the string. 2. Someone listens with eyes shut and says which instrument is playing. 3. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Play the tune on the bottles, then on the string. I will shut my eyes. The notes are the same. So how can I still tell which instrument it is?
flow.kid: Play your tune on the bottles. Then play it on the string. Can a listener tell them apart?

ask.q: How did you raise the note of the bottle? How did you raise the note of the string?
good: I made the air column shorter with more water.
I made the string shorter with the pencil.

ask.q: The two instruments played the same notes. Did they sound the same?
good: No. The bottle hoots and the string twangs.
The pitch was the same, and the kind of sound was different.

flow.parent: Two instruments at the same pitch have the same main frequency. They still sound different, because each adds its own mix of weaker, higher vibrations. That mix is called timbre, and it is a third measure of a sound.
flow.context: This is the last step of Two Instruments, One Tune. You play one tune on the tuned bottles and on the Water-Bottle String, and compare them.

challenges.title: One String, Five Notes: an instrument heard across the room
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You build an instrument with only one string. It must play five different notes, and a listener four big steps away must hear every one.
challenges.problem: Build an instrument with one string that can play five different notes, going up in order. A listener four big steps away must be able to hear each note clearly. You have 30 minutes and things from around your home.
constraints: Only one string, or one rubber band, may vibrate.
The five notes must go up in order. You must be able to play them again in the same order.
No phone, speaker or amplifier may be used to make it louder.
A listener four big steps away must hear every note.
materials: about 2 metres of thin strong string, or large rubber bands
an empty box, a steel dabba, a plastic tub or a bucket
pencils, a ruler and sticky tape
a bottle of water to use as a weight
a paper cup or a steel tumbler
general: Stretch the string over a hollow box, with a pencil under each end as a bridge. The box is the soundboard.
Mark five places along the string. Press the string down at each mark, or slide a pencil to it, to make the vibrating part shorter.
Tie one end of the string to a pencil. Turn the pencil like a peg to tighten the string for each note.
creative: Turn a plastic bucket upside down. Thread the string through a small hole in its base and knot it inside. Tie the other end to the top of a stick that stands on the bucket. Lean the stick back to tighten the string.
Slide a steel tumbler along the string as you pluck. A chitravina player slides a smooth block along the strings in this way.
Thread the string through the bottom of a paper cup, so that the cup pushes the air.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own instrument. Draw it first and mark how you will get five notes. Build it and test it with a listener four big steps away. Write which idea changed the pitch, which idea changed the volume, and what you would change next time.

setup.art: A single string lying on a table beside an empty shoe box, a bucket, two pencils and a bottle of water.
setup.caption: 1. Look at what you have: one string and things from around the home.

setup.art: A string stretched over a shoe box with a pencil under each end and five pencil marks along the box beside the string.
setup.caption: 2. Find a way to get five notes, and a way to make them loud enough.

setup.art: A child plucking the finished instrument while a second person stands four steps away with a hand raised to show they can hear.
setup.caption: 3. Test it with a listener four big steps away.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem and the four rules aloud. 2. Your child plucks the bare string, held tight between two hands by a helper. 3. The listener stands four big steps away and says whether they can hear it. 4. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Here is the problem. One string, five notes, heard from four steps away. A bare string is very quiet. Why? And what could change its note?
flow.kid: Read the problem. Pluck the bare string. Can the listener hear it? What must you change?

ask.q: What will you change to get five different notes?
good: The length of the string.
How tight the string is.

ask.q: What will you change to make it louder?
good: Put it on a hollow box.
Pluck it harder.

flow.parent: A thin string pushes very little air, so it is quiet without a soundboard. Pitch and volume need two separate fixes.
flow.context: This is the first step of One String, Five Notes. You hear how quiet a bare string is, and think about what could change its volume and its pitch.

flow.do: 1. Read the usual ideas together: a box, marks along the string, and a pencil as a peg. 2. Your child chooses, draws a plan and builds it. 3. They test the five notes with the listener. 4. They change one thing at a time and test again.
flow.say: Which idea will you use for the notes, and which for the loudness? Why do you think it will work? Change one thing at a time, so you know what helped.
flow.kid: Pick an idea for the notes. Pick an idea for the loudness. Build it. Test it. Change one thing.
flow.parent: A grown-up makes any hole in a box or a bucket. If the notes are too close together to tell apart, make the steps in length bigger.
flow.context: In this step of One String, Five Notes you build your instrument. You test whether it plays five notes that a listener can hear from four big steps away.

flow.do: 1. Read the creative ideas together. 2. Your child tries one, or adds it to their instrument. 3. They play the five notes for the listener, up and then down. 4. They write what changed the pitch and what changed the volume.
flow.say: Here are three unusual ideas. Which one would you like to try? When you have finished, play me your five notes, up and then down.
flow.kid: Read the unusual ideas. Try one. Play your five notes up and down. Write what you changed.

ask.q: In your instrument, what sets the pitch, and what sets the volume?
good: The length or the tension of the string sets the pitch.
The box or the bucket, and how hard I pluck, set the volume.

flow.parent: The upturned bucket is often the loudest, because its wide base is a large soundboard. Leaning the stick changes the tension, so the note slides.
flow.context: This is the last step of One String, Five Notes. You try an unusual idea, play your five notes, and write what set the pitch and what set the volume.

worksheets.title: Loud or quiet, high or low (core)

items.p: What does the volume of a sound tell you?
opts: How loud or quiet it is
How high or low it is
items.why: Volume is loudness. Choosing 'how high or low' mixes volume up with pitch, which is the other measure of a sound.

items.p: What does the pitch of a sound depend on?
opts: The number of vibrations each second
items.why: Pitch depends on the frequency, which is the number of vibrations each second. The size of each vibration is the amplitude, and it sets the volume.

items.p: True or false: plucking a string harder gives a higher note.
items.why: False. In Gentle Pluck, Hard Pluck, a bigger pull gave a louder sound at the same number of hertz. A harder pluck changes the amplitude, and the frequency stays the same.

items.p: Volume is measured in ____, and frequency is measured in ____.
items.why: The decibel is the unit of volume. The hertz is the unit of frequency, and one hertz is one vibration each second.

items.p: Match each sound to its volume and pitch.
items.why: All four mixes of volume and pitch exist. That shows the two measures are separate.

items.p: Sort these actions by what they change: the volume or the pitch.
items: wrapping a phone in a towel
opening a hole on a bansuri
items.why: Volume changes with the amplitude, with covers and with distance. Pitch changes with the tension, length and weight of a string, and with the length of an air column.

items.p: Put these sounds in order, from the quietest to the loudest.
items.why: Leaves are about 20 decibels, a whisper about 30 and talking about 60. A mixie is about 85 to 90, and a horn close by about 100.

items.p: How many times the sound energy of 60 decibels does a sound of 70 decibels have?
items.why: Every 10 decibels more means ten times the sound energy. If you wrote 10 more, or a little more, you read the scale as adding. It multiplies.

items.p: Which change makes the note of a string higher?
items.why: A tighter string is pulled back harder, so it vibrates faster. A longer or heavier string vibrates more slowly. A gentle pluck only makes the sound quieter.

items.p: True or false: a shorter air column gives a lower note.
items.why: False. In the Filling Bottle, the note rose as the air column above the water got shorter. A shorter air column vibrates faster.

items.p: A phone plays a tune under four layers of towel. What does the towel change, and what stays the same?
items.a: The towel makes the tune quieter, because it absorbs some of the sound energy. It does not change the pitch of any note, so the tune is still the same tune.
items.why: A strong answer names both measures. It says that the volume falls and the pitch stays. It uses the word 'absorb' or says where the energy goes.

items.p: Explain why sounds above 85 decibels are a danger. Name two ways to protect your ears.
items.a: Loud sound over many hours damages the hair cells of the inner ear, and they do not grow back. To protect my ears I can move further away, turn the volume down or spend less time near the sound. I can also wear earplugs or earmuffs.
items.why: A strong answer says that the harm builds up with loudness and time, and that it does not heal. It gives two real protections.

items.p: Draw one string twice: for a quiet sound, and for a loud sound of the same pitch. Label the amplitude.
items.a: Two strings of the same length between the same fixed ends. The quiet one is a narrow blur. The loud one is a wide blur. On each, an arrow from the rest position to the edge of the blur is labelled 'amplitude'.
items.why: A strong drawing keeps the length the same in both pictures, because the pitch is the same. Only the width of the blur differs.
items.art: Two pairs of fixed pegs, one above the other, with blank space between each pair for the child's drawing.

items.p: Should loudspeakers at a festival be switched off at 10 at night?

views.says: The festival comes once a year. The music brings the whole street together, and most people enjoy it.

views.who: A parent of a new baby
views.says: A baby, a person who is ill and a worker on an early shift all need sleep. Sound above the limit, hour after hour, harms them.
Birds roosting in the trees and other animals hear it too. They cannot shut a window or move to another room.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from what you found in this unit. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. One reason is that sound above 85 decibels harms hearing over hours. Another is that every 10 decibels less means only a tenth of the energy. So turning down a little helps a lot. A third is that the music can go on at a lower volume.
items.why: Each view has something right in it. A strong answer uses a fact about decibels, and it looks for a way that meets more than one need.

items.p: In which family of instruments does an air column vibrate?
items.why: In a bansuri or a nadaswaram, the air inside the tube vibrates. In string instruments, strings vibrate. In drums, a tight skin vibrates.

worksheets.title: Changing the pitch and changing the volume (stretch)

items.p: A string gives 110 hertz. The pull on it is made four times as great. What is the new frequency?
items.why: Four times the pull doubles the frequency, and 110 × 2 = 220. If you wrote 440, you multiplied by four. The frequency grows more slowly than the pull.

items.p: A string 40 cm long is shortened to 20 cm, with the same pull. What happens to its frequency?
opts: It becomes four times as high
items.why: Half the length gives twice the frequency. If you chose 'halves', you matched a shorter string to a smaller number. A shorter string vibrates faster.

items.p: Why does a thick string give a lower note than a thin one of the same length and tension?
opts: It has more weight to move
items.why: A heavier string takes longer over each trip, so it vibrates more slowly. In the Water-Bottle String, a string with a second strand wound on it gave a lower note.

items.p: True or false: a wooden soundboard adds energy to the sound of a string.
items.why: False. The soundboard pushes more air than the thin string can, so the string's energy reaches the air faster. Only an amplifier adds energy, from a battery or the mains.

items.p: Three of these raise the pitch of a drum. Which one lowers it?
opts: Drying the skin under a lamp
items.why: Water loosens a skin, and a looser skin vibrates more slowly. Tightening, drying and a smaller skin all make the skin vibrate faster.

items.p: A machine that makes a weak electric signal stronger, using energy from the mains, is an ____.
items.why: An amplifier takes the weak signal from a microphone and makes it strong enough to drive a loudspeaker.

items.p: Sort these by how they make a sound quieter: by absorbing it, by blocking it, or by spreading it out.
items: a pillow over an alarm clock
moving the radio to the far end of a hall
items.why: Soft, thick things absorb sound and turn it into a tiny amount of warmth. Heavy, hard things block it. Distance spreads the same energy over more space.

items.p: Four bottles have air columns of these lengths. Put them in order, from the lowest note to the highest.
items.why: The longest air column vibrates most slowly and gives the lowest note. The shortest gives the highest.

items.p: One singer reads 60 decibels on a sound meter. About how many decibels do ten equal singers read?
items.why: Ten singers send out ten times the energy, and ten times the energy is 10 decibels more. 60 + 10 = 70. It is not 600, because decibels count multiplications.

items.p: Stretching a rubber band makes it much tighter, yet its note hardly rises. Explain why.
items.a: Stretching changes three things at once. The band gets tighter and thinner, which raise the note. It also gets longer, which lowers the note. The changes nearly cancel.
items.why: A strong answer names all three changes and says which way each one pushes the note. It may add that this is why a fair test changes one thing only.

items.p: In the Muffle Test, a phone plays a tune under different covers. Name the independent, dependent and two control variables.
items.a: The independent variable is the cover. The dependent variable is the reading in decibels. Control variables are the tune, the volume setting, the two phones and the 50 cm between them.
items.why: A strong answer gives one thing changed, one thing measured, and at least two things kept the same.

items.p: A bansuri player opens one more hole. Explain what happens to the air column and to the note.
items.a: The air column now ends at the open hole, so it is shorter. A shorter air column vibrates faster, so the note is higher.
items.why: A strong answer links the hole to the length of the air column, and the length to the frequency.

items.p: A noisy classroom disturbs the class next door. Which fix is best?

views.says: Ask everyone to speak more softly. The sound is weakest when it is never made.
Hang thick curtains and pin up soft boards. They absorb the sound inside the room.
Close the gaps round the door first. A gap lets more sound through than the whole wall does.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from what you found in this unit. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. In the Muffle Test, four layers of towel absorbed more than one layer. A gap of one finger-width in the dabba's lid let a lot of sound out. Making less sound at the source helps every listener.
items.why: Each view works on a different part of the path: the source, the room and the leaks. A strong answer uses evidence from the Muffle Test and may combine two fixes.

items.p: Label this veena: string, peg, fret, hollow body. Write 'pitch' or 'volume' beside each part that changes one.
a: Peg: changes the pitch, by changing the tension
Fret: changes the pitch, by making the vibrating part shorter
Hollow body: changes the volume, as a soundboard
items.why: The pegs and the frets set the pitch through tension and length. The hollow body pushes more air than the string can, so it sets how loud the veena is.
items.art: An outline drawing of a veena seen from the front, with four blank label lines pointing to a string, a tuning peg, a fret and the round hollow body.

items.p: True or false: as a plucked string's sound fades away, its pitch drops lower and lower.
items.why: False. In Gentle Pluck, Hard Pluck, the blur got narrower as the sound faded. The tuner showed the same number of hertz. A fading sound loses amplitude and keeps its frequency.

worksheets.title: Testing ideas about volume and pitch (challenge)

items.p: A tuner reads 220 hertz beside a steady humming string. What does it read from across the room?
items.why: Distance lowers the volume and leaves the frequency alone. Every push that leaves the string still arrives, so the pushes arrive just as often.

items.p: Two equal loudspeakers play together. How does the meter reading compare with one alone?
items.why: Two equal sources give twice the energy, and twice the energy is only about 3 decibels more. It takes ten times the energy to add 10 decibels.

items.p: True or false: a sound of 80 decibels has twice the energy of a sound of 40 decibels.
items.why: False. Each 10 decibels is ten times the energy. From 40 to 80 is four steps: 10 × 10 × 10 × 10, which is 10,000 times the energy.

items.p: True or false: a sound can be strong in the air and still be silent to a human listener.
items.why: True. Ultrasound above 20,000 hertz and infrasound below 20 hertz can carry plenty of energy. Human ears do not respond to them, though a dog or an elephant may hear them well.

items.p: Match each instrument to the way its player gets a higher note.
pairs: Presses a string on a fret
Taps the blocks to tighten the skin
items.why: A fret shortens the string. An open hole shortens the air column. Tapping the blocks tightens the skin. A harmonium has a separate reed for every note.

items.p: A string gives 150 hertz when 60 cm of it vibrates. What does it give at 30 cm?
items.why: 30 cm is half of 60 cm. With the same pull, half the length gives twice the frequency, and 150 × 2 = 300.

items.p: Sound below 20 hertz is called ____, and sound above 20,000 hertz is called ____.
items.why: Elephants call with infrasound, and bats find insects with ultrasound. Both lie outside the range of human hearing.

items.p: Near thunder has a sharp crack. Far thunder is only a low rumble. Why?
opts: Air weakens high notes more than low notes
The pitch of every note drops with distance
Low notes travel faster than high notes
Thunder slows down on the way
items.why: Air absorbs high frequencies more than low ones, so only the low part of the sound arrives from far away. The notes that arrive still have the frequency they started with.

items.p: Many people think a drum sounds higher when it is hit harder. Describe a fair test of this idea.
items.a: Hit the same drum in the same place with the same stick, gently and then hard, three times each. Hold a tuner app in the same place and read the frequency each time. Change only the strength of the hit. If the hertz stay the same, the idea is wrong.
items.why: A strong answer changes one thing and measures the frequency, not the loudness. It keeps the drum, the stick and the place the same, and repeats each hit.

items.p: English speakers call a pitch 'high'. Farsi speakers call it 'thin'. Which word fits the science better? Give a reason.
items.a: Either word, with a reason. 'Thin' fits because thin strings and small things do give higher notes. 'High' fits because the frequency is a higher number. Nothing in the sound is higher up, so both are borrowed words for a faster vibration.
items.why: A strong answer says what a high pitch really is, a higher frequency, and tests each word against that.

items.p: A sound meter reads 60 decibels for a low hum and for a high beep. Will they sound equally loud?
items.a: Not always. The meter measures the strength of the sound in the air. Human ears are less sensitive to low sounds, so the low hum may sound quieter than the beep. Fletcher and Munson showed this in 1933.
items.why: A strong answer separates the strength in the air from the loudness a listener hears. It says that the ear's sensitivity depends on pitch.

items.p: A phone on a table plays a song. Give three ways to make it louder without the volume button.
items.a: Stand the phone in an empty steel tumbler or a cone, which sends the sound one way. Rest it on a hollow wooden box, which acts as a soundboard. Move closer to it. None of these adds energy. Only an amplifier would.
items.why: A strong answer gives three working ways. It says that each one only gathers or passes on the energy the phone already gives out.

items.p: Is loudness in the air, or in the listener?

views.says: The strength of a sound is a fact about the air. A meter can measure it in an empty room.
Loudness is made by an ear and a brain. The same strength is loud at one pitch and faint at another.
A strong low sound can be felt through the floor and in the chest. A body meets sound in more ways than by hearing.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from what you found in this unit. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. The meter in the Muffle Test gave numbers with nobody listening closely. A dog whistle is strong in the air and silent to a human. A low hum and a high beep with the same reading do not sound equally loud.
items.why: No view is simply wrong. A strong answer separates what a meter measures from what someone hears, and gives one example.

items.p: Draw a quiet box for a noisy ticking clock. Label what absorbs, what blocks, and where sound might leak.
items.a: A box with a heavy wall, such as a steel dabba or a thick wooden box, labelled 'blocks'. A soft lining, such as folded towel or sponge, labelled 'absorbs'. The lid closes with no gap. The join of the lid is marked as the place a leak might be. The clock stands on a soft pad.
items.why: A strong design uses both a heavy wall and a soft lining, and closes every gap. It keeps the clock from touching the hard wall.
items.art: A blank space with a small ticking clock drawn in one corner, ready for the child's design.

items.p: Put these in order of frequency, from the lowest to the highest.
items: The highest sound a bat hears
a: The highest sound a bat hears
items.why: The elephant's rumble is about 15 hertz and a man's voice about 120. A mosquito's whine is about 500 and a cricket's chirp about 5,000. Many bats hear up to about 110,000.

quiz.p: A sound gets louder, and its note stays the same. What has changed?
quiz.why: A louder sound comes from a bigger amplitude. The frequency sets the pitch, and the pitch did not change.

quiz.p: Which pair of units is right?
opts: Volume in decibels, frequency in hertz
Volume in hertz, frequency in decibels
Volume in metres, frequency in seconds
quiz.why: Decibels measure volume. Hertz measure frequency, the number of vibrations each second.

quiz.p: Which of these sounds is quiet and high-pitched?
quiz.why: A mosquito's whine is quiet and about 500 hertz. A chenda is loud and low, a whistle is loud and high, and a far lorry is quiet and low.

quiz.p: A reading goes from 50 decibels to 60 decibels. How much more sound energy is that?
quiz.why: Every 10 decibels more is ten times the energy. If you chose 'a fifth more', you treated decibels like centimetres. The scale multiplies.

quiz.p: Which of these sounds can harm hearing if it goes on for hours?
quiz.why: A mixie at one metre is about 85 to 90 decibels. Sounds above 85 decibels can damage the inner ear over hours. The others are far below that.

quiz.p: A hanging bottle of water pulls a string tight. Which change gives a lower note?
quiz.why: Less water means less tension, and a looser string vibrates more slowly. A shorter or thinner string is higher. A gentle pluck is only quieter.

quiz.p: How much more pull does it take to double the frequency of a string?
quiz.why: Four times the pull doubles the frequency. Twice the pull raises it only about 1.4 times. The Water-Bottle String shows this.

quiz.p: Water is poured into a tall bottle, and the sound of the pouring rises. Why?
quiz.why: The air above the water is what vibrates. As the bottle fills, the air column gets shorter and vibrates faster.

quiz.p: What does a wooden soundboard do for a string?
opts: It pushes more air, making the sound louder
It adds energy from the wood
It makes the string vibrate faster
It makes the note last longer
quiz.why: A thin string moves little air. The wide board vibrates with it and pushes far more air. It adds no energy, and it does not change the frequency.

quiz.p: True or false: a narrow gap under a door lets very little sound through.
quiz.why: False. In the Muffle Test, opening the dabba's lid by one finger-width sent the reading up a lot. Sound gets through any gap.

quiz.p: In a fair test of covers for a ringing phone, which is the independent variable?
quiz.why: The independent variable is the one thing changed on purpose. The reading in decibels is measured, so it is the dependent variable. The tune and the distance are kept the same.

quiz.p: A song comes faintly through a wall. What about it has not changed?
quiz.why: A wall takes energy from the sound, so it is quieter and duller. The frequency of each note that gets through is the same as when it was sung.

applications: Makers of veenas, sitars and violins choose the thickness of each string and the tension it will carry. In this way every string gives its own note at the same length.
India's Noise Pollution Rules of 2000 set limits in decibels. In places where people live, the limit is 55 decibels by day and 45 by night.
Workers in factories, airports and building sites wear earmuffs. A hard shell blocks sound, and soft foam inside absorbs it.
Cinema halls and recording studios line their walls with soft panels and thick curtains. These absorb sound, so that it does not bounce around.
A hearing aid has a tiny microphone, an amplifier and a loudspeaker. It is set to add most volume at the pitches its wearer hears least well.
Doctors use ultrasound, far above 20,000 hertz, to make pictures of a baby before birth. The sound is too high for anyone to hear.
Elephants call in infrasound, because low frequencies are weakened least by air and forest. A herd can keep in touch over several kilometres.
