open_questions.q: Why do a few people have perfect pitch, and name any note they hear?
open_questions.why_open: It runs in some families, and it is more common in people who began music very young. It is also more common among speakers of languages that use pitch to tell words apart. Nobody knows how much is inborn and how much is learned.

open_questions.q: Can the hair cells of a human inner ear be made to grow back?
open_questions.why_open: Birds and fish regrow these cells after loud sound damages them. Humans and other mammals do not. Scientists are trying to find out what switches the regrowth on, and no treatment works yet.

open_questions.q: How much does the noise of ships harm whales and other sea animals?
open_questions.why_open: The sea has become much louder at low frequencies, where large whales call. Some whales call louder or leave noisy places. How much this harms their feeding and their young is still being measured.

open_questions.q: Do plants respond to the pitch of the sounds around them?
open_questions.why_open: In a 2019 study, evening primrose flowers made sweeter nectar within minutes of hearing a bee's low buzz. High-pitched sounds had no such effect. Few other teams have repeated this yet.

open_questions.q: Are babies born linking pitch to height, or do they learn it from words?
open_questions.why_open: In 2014, a study tested babies of four months. They matched a rising pitch to a rising ball, and also to a thinning tube. How language later strengthens one link and weakens the other is still being studied.

ask_kids: Listen to the pressure cooker, the doorbell and the fridge. Which is the loudest? Which has the highest pitch? Are they the same one?
Fill your water bottle at the tap with your eyes shut. How do you know when to stop?
When you call someone far away, do you make your voice louder, higher or both? Why?
Why do you think an auto's horn is high-pitched and a lorry's horn is low?
A song is playing in the next flat. You can still tell which song it is. What reached you, and what got lost on the way?
Whose voice in our family is the lowest? Whose is the highest? What might be different in their throats?
If the whole street shouted together, would it be a thousand times as loud as one person?
Which sounds do you think the street dog hears that we do not?

maths.problem: In the Water-Bottle String, 250 grams of water gave 110 hertz, and 1,000 grams gave 220 hertz. How much water would give 440 hertz?
maths.answer: 4,000 grams, which is 4 kilograms or 4 litres of water.
maths.explain: From 250 to 1,000 grams the pull became 4 times as great, and the frequency doubled. To double it again, from 220 to 440, the pull must become 4 times as great again. 1,000 × 4 = 4,000 grams.
maths.context: In the Water-Bottle String, a bottle of water hangs from a string and pulls it tight. More water gives a higher note. These numbers are made-up example results.
maths.why_maths: The pattern lets you predict a weight you cannot safely hang on a thin string, without trying it.

maths.problem: A string gives 155 hertz when 40 cm of it vibrates. What will it give at 20 cm, and at 10 cm? What fraction of 40 cm is each length?
maths.answer: 310 hertz at 20 cm, which is one half of 40 cm. 620 hertz at 10 cm, which is one quarter of 40 cm.
maths.explain: Half the length gives twice the frequency: 155 × 2 = 310. A quarter of the length gives four times the frequency: 155 × 4 = 620. The fraction of the length and the multiple of the frequency are a matching pair: one half and 2, one quarter and 4.
maths.context: In the Water-Bottle String, you slide a pencil to make the vibrating part of the string shorter. A shorter string gives a higher note.
maths.why_maths: Fractions of the length tell a veena maker exactly where to put each fret.

maths.problem: A whisper is 30 decibels and a mixie is 90 decibels. How many times the sound energy of the whisper does the mixie have?
maths.explain: Every 10 decibels more is 10 times the energy. From 30 to 90 is 60 decibels, which is 6 steps of 10. So multiply by 10 six times: 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000,000.
maths.context: In the Sound Grid, you measure sounds in your home in decibels. Every 10 decibels more means ten times as much sound energy.
maths.why_maths: Ears cope with sounds a million times stronger than a whisper. Counting in steps of ten times keeps the numbers small enough to use.

maths.problem: In the Muffle Test, the readings in decibels were 70 with no cover and 66 with one layer of towel. They were 60 with four layers, 54 in the closed dabba and 64 with the lid a little open. Draw a bar chart. How many decibels did each cover take away?
maths.answer: One layer took away 4 decibels and four layers took away 10. The closed dabba took away 16, and the dabba with its lid a little open took away 6.
maths.explain: Subtract each reading from 70. 70 − 66 = 4. 70 − 60 = 10. 70 − 54 = 16. 70 − 64 = 6. Four layers took away 10 decibels, so only a tenth of the sound energy got through.
maths.context: In the Muffle Test, a phone plays a tune under different covers. A sound meter 50 cm away reads the volume. These numbers are made-up example results.
maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows at a glance which cover muffled best. It also shows how much the small gap in the lid spoiled the dabba.

maths.problem: In Gentle Pluck, Hard Pluck, pulls of half a centimetre, 1 cm and 2 cm were made. They gave 48, 54 and 60 decibels. What is the pattern? Predict the reading for a pull of 4 cm. Why might the real reading be different?
maths.answer: Each time the pull doubles, the reading goes up by 6 decibels. The pattern predicts 66 decibels for 4 cm. The real reading may differ, because a string pulled that far can hit the table or slip on the pencils.
maths.explain: 54 − 48 = 6 and 60 − 54 = 6. The pull doubled each time: half, 1, 2. Doubling again gives 4 cm, and 60 + 6 = 66. A pattern holds only as far as the thing keeps behaving in the same way.
maths.context: In Gentle Pluck, Hard Pluck, you pull a string aside by measured distances. You read the loudness on a sound meter. These numbers are made-up example results.
maths.why_maths: A rule that links what goes in to what comes out lets you predict. Then you can check where the rule stops working.

maths.problem: A bottle is 24 cm tall. Water fills it to 6 cm, then 12 cm, then 18 cm. How long is the air column each time? What fraction of the bottle is air?
maths.answer: 18 cm, which is three quarters. 12 cm, which is one half. 6 cm, which is one quarter.
maths.explain: Subtract the height of the water from 24 cm. 24 − 6 = 18, 24 − 12 = 12, and 24 − 18 = 6. Out of 24, 18 is three quarters, 12 is one half and 6 is one quarter. The shortest air column, 6 cm, gives the highest note.
maths.context: In the Filling Bottle, water is poured into a tall bottle. The air column above the water gets shorter, and the note of the pouring rises.
maths.why_maths: The note depends on the air and not on the water, so you need the length that is left over.

maths.problem: Three readings of one note on a tuner were 152, 155 and 157 hertz. A fourth reading was 310 hertz. Which reading should be checked again, and why?
maths.answer: The reading of 310 hertz. It is exactly twice 155.
maths.explain: Three readings lie within 5 hertz of each other. The fourth is double. A tuner app sometimes catches a higher part of the sound, at twice the main frequency. Pluck again, gently, at the middle of the string.
maths.context: In the Water-Bottle String, you read the frequency of a plucked string from a tuner app. You take three readings for each test.
maths.why_maths: Repeating a measurement shows which reading is the odd one. The size of the oddness can hint at its cause.

quiz: Plucking a string harder makes its note higher.
It makes the sound louder. The frequency stays the same.
Volume is measured in decibels.
Every 10 decibels more is ten times the sound energy.
A tighter string gives a higher note.
It is pulled back harder, so it vibrates faster.
Twice the pull on a string gives twice the frequency.
It takes four times the pull to double the frequency.
A longer air column gives a higher note.
A longer air column vibrates more slowly and gives a lower note.
A towel over a phone changes the pitch of its tune.

A wooden soundboard adds energy to a string's sound.

Sounds above 85 decibels can harm hearing over hours.

how_we_found_out.context: Is a sound with more energy always louder? This card tells how two scientists tested that idea, and how it turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: By the 1920s, telephone engineers in America could measure the strength of a sound with instruments. It seemed natural that strength and loudness were the same thing. Two sounds of the same strength should then sound equally loud. Harvey Fletcher and Wilden Munson, at Bell Telephone Laboratories in New York, tested this. Listeners wore earphones and heard two tones in turn. One tone was always 1,000 hertz. The other was lower or higher. Its strength was changed until the listener judged both tones equally loud. Then the scientists compared the two strengths. The idea failed. A quiet tone of 100 hertz needed about a hundred times the energy of the 1,000 hertz tone. Only then did it seem as loud. Human ears were most sensitive at about 3,000 to 4,000 hertz. Fletcher and Munson published their curves in 1933. Later teams measured again with more listeners, and the curves changed a little. The main finding held. Loudness depends on pitch as well as on strength. Sound meters today count low sounds less, as human ears do.
how_we_found_out.who: Harvey Fletcher and Wilden Munson, American scientists at Bell Telephone Laboratories
how_we_found_out.when: They published their results in 1933. Other teams measured again in 1956 and in 2003.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That two sounds of the same strength always sound equally loud. Fletcher and Munson showed that a low tone needs far more energy than a middle tone to sound as loud. Human ears are less sensitive to low sounds.

playtest: Read through as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, step by step. The experiments were reasoned through carefully, but they have not yet been tried at home. Treat the expected results as likely, and write down what really happens. The Water-Bottle String (core) needs a thin string that hardly stretches, a table with a leg or a grille to tie to, a 1-litre bottle and a phone with a free tuner app. Sewing thread snaps under a full bottle. The note is soft, so the room must be quiet. With a string of 40 cm, the readings should lie somewhere between 100 and 350 hertz, and they should rise with each amount of water by smaller steps than the water does. Friction where the string bends over the table edge can change a reading by several hertz, so the bag is lifted and lowered before each pluck. The winding of a second strand may buzz. Without a tuner app the notes can only be put in order by ear, and the 'four times the pull' result cannot be checked. Gentle Pluck, Hard Pluck (core) uses the same string. Phone sound meters are rough, and a single pluck is short, so the highest reading is used. The order of the three readings is reliable, and the step of 6 decibels is only approximate. The Muffle Test (core) needs two phones. The order of the towel and the dabba may differ from the example table, and the unit says so. The drop for four layers of towel and the rise when the lid is opened are the reliable results. The phone plays at half volume, 50 cm from the meter, and nobody puts an ear near it. The Filling Bottle (core) works best with a tall, narrow bottle and a thin, steady stream. The Sound Grid measures every sound from 1 metre or more, and the mixie from 2 metres for 5 seconds. In the Rubber Band Puzzle, bands differ: most rise a little in pitch and then level off, and the note says so. Blowing across a bottle in Two Instruments, One Tune takes a few minutes of practice, and matching a string to a bottle by ear takes patience. No part needs a garden, a pet or a musical instrument. Facts to treat with care: the frequencies of voices, wings and animal hearing are rounded and vary a great deal. Decibel values for home sounds are typical figures.
